options.A: Which plan will look neater in my report to the area manager?
options.B: Which plan makes the customer's outcome more certain?
options.C: Which plan is easier for the team to run on the day?
options.D: Which plan would head office prefer to see on the floor?

questions.stem:
A customer comes to the till angry. His sofa was delivered damaged, and this is his third visit about it. He says, "Do something."
What is the best response?

options.A: "Three visits and a damaged sofa: you're right to be angry. I'm booking a replacement now and will call you Wednesday by noon."
options.B: "Damage has to be reported within two days. Let me check whether you did that."
options.C: "I'll sort everything out: a replacement, a full refund and a voucher, all today, no problem."
options.D: "I understand it's frustrating, but delays happen with every delivery, and it is not unusual."

questions.stem:
A new manager drafts a 30-day plan with five priorities. One reads: "Improve stock accuracy. Owner: the store. Check: end of month."
What is the best fix?

options.A: Keep all five, because a full month is long enough to make progress on every area.
options.B: Leave the line as it is, and share it with the team out loud rather than in writing.
options.C: Cut to no more than three, and give the stock line a measurable goal, a named owner and one behavior.
options.D: Keep five, but write each one in fewer words so that the whole plan reads quickly.

questions.stem:
Your 30-day plan has conversion as a priority, with a goal of 20 percent. At day 25 it is at 17. In the middle of the month, head office changed the price of your top-selling line. Your manager asks for an update.
Which update is best?

options.A: "We would have hit 20 percent by now, but head office changed the price of our top-selling line in the middle of the month."
options.B: "It may well recover on its own once customers get used to the new price, so I'll report when it does."
options.C: "The team has worked very hard in a month when the price change made the goal unrealistic for everyone."
options.D: "Conversion is 17 against 20. The price change was outside my control; what I own is our response, a greeting question at that aisle. I recommend we review the goal. I need your decision by Friday."

questions.stem:
Rana wants to know whether her listening and her matching of offers to needs are improving week by week.
Which number should she watch most closely?

options.A: Calls made, because more dials in a week show more effort and more chances taken.
options.B: Contact rate, because it shows how often her dials actually reach a person.
options.C: Average order value, because bigger orders always mean she listened better.
options.D: Conversion: the share of real conversations that end in the outcome.

questions.stem:
Karim's conversion is the best on the team, but his average order value is the lowest. Several of his customers call back within a month to move to a bigger plan.
What does this most likely tell you?

options.A: He should make more dials, because volume is what is holding his numbers back.
options.B: He is often recommending less than the customer really needs.
options.C: His contact rate must be low, so he keeps reaching the wrong people.
options.D: Nothing important, since conversion is the only number that reflects skill.

questions.stem:
Before a one-hour session, a rep writes her goal at the top of the page.
Which is the best session goal?

options.A: "Make as many calls as I can before five o'clock."
options.B: "Get through all 40 names on today's list."
options.C: "Book two meetings with small business owners."
options.D: "Sell harder than yesterday and close more deals."

questions.stem:
Omar calls a past customer whose broadband contract with his company ends this month. The customer is on an approved list.
Which opening is best?

options.A: "Hello, this is Omar from Brightwave. I know this call is unexpected, so if now is a bad time, just say so. I'm calling because your contract with us ends this month. How has the connection been for you lately?"
options.B: "Hi, how are you today? I'll be quick. I'm Omar from Brightwave, and we have a great deal I think you'll love. Have you got a minute to hear it?"
options.C: "Hello, Omar from Brightwave. Your contract ends this month, and we have some new plans. Would you like to hear about them now?"
options.D: "Hello, this is Omar from Brightwave. If now is a bad time, just say. Everyone on your street is switching to our new plan, so I wanted to make sure you don't miss out."

questions.stem:
You end your opener with an open question, and the line goes quiet for a couple of seconds.
What should you do?

options.A: Answer your own question, so the silence does not start to feel awkward.
options.B: Wait. The pause is space for the other person to think.
options.C: Fill the gap with the main benefits of the offer while you have their attention.
options.D: Ask, "Are you still there?" and repeat the whole opener a little faster.

questions.stem:
A woman calls the mobile line and says she wants to add a second SIM for her teenage son. On your screen you can see a family bundle, a TV add-on and phone insurance.
What is the best next step?

options.A: Mention the family bundle, the TV add-on and the insurance, so she knows everything you offer.
options.B: Read her the current promotion first, since it may change what she wants today.
options.C: Ask for her name again and run through the full standard script before anything else.
options.D: Ask a little about how her son will use the phone, and understand that first.

questions.stem:
A shop owner says, "Not a good time." You give one calm line with your true reason and offer to let her go. She says, "Really, not now."
What do you do?

options.A: Thank her and close honestly, offering to call at a time that suits her.
options.B: Read out the main points of the offer quickly, before she has a chance to hang up.
options.C: Tell her it will only take a minute, so that she stays on the line a little longer.
options.D: Make the same push a third time, more slowly, so that she finally hears your reason.

questions.stem:
After your opener, a small business owner says, "Honestly, our deliveries are a mess every Monday."
What is the best next move?

options.A: Now that there is interest, explain your delivery service and its main features in full.
options.B: Ask four quick questions in a row about volume, drivers, routes and costs.
options.C: Say back what you heard in a few words, ask one short open question, then stop.
options.D: Say, "So you're busy on Mondays. Would our delivery service help with that?"

questions.stem:
A client says, "We lose half a morning chasing unpaid invoices."
What should your note say?

options.A: "lose half a morning chasing unpaid invoices"
options.B: "invoicing inefficiency"
options.C: "busy mornings"
options.D: "interested in product"

questions.stem:
You want a sense of a small firm's budget without making the owner defensive.
Which question fits the course?

options.A: "What is your budget for this?"
options.B: "How much are you willing to spend each month?"
options.C: "Most firms your size choose between a smaller starting option and a fuller one. Which sounds more like you?"
options.D: "Our plans start at 90 a month. Can you afford that?"

questions.stem:
On a phone call, a rep reads out all four plans in detail. The client says, "Let me think about it."
What is the most likely reason?

options.A: The client is not interested and is ending the call politely.
options.B: The price of every plan is too high for the client's budget.
options.C: The client needs to hear about more plans before deciding.
options.D: Too many options with nothing to look at stalled the decision.

questions.stem:
Earlier in the call, the client said, "I'm sick of the system crashing every Friday." Now she says, "Another company quoted us less."
What is the best response?

options.A: "I understand, but our servers are faster and our support team runs around the clock."
options.B: (pause) "That's fair. Price matters. The question I'd ask is what those Friday crashes cost you now. What would need to be true for this to be worth it?"
options.C: "I can take ten percent off if you sign today, so that we beat their quote."
options.D: "That's fair, price matters. So would you like to go ahead with us anyway?"

questions.stem:
A client says, "That's a lot." The rep stays quiet for two slow breaths, and the client adds, "Our last provider promised the same and let us down."
What did the pause do?

options.A: It made the client uncomfortable, which pressured him into talking.
options.B: It gave the rep time to prepare a full list of features to answer with.
options.C: It gave the client room to say the real reason behind the objection.
options.D: It signalled doubt, so the client tried to reassure the rep.

questions.stem:
You are allowed to waive the setup fee. A client asks, "Can you do something on the price?"
What do you do?

options.A: Offer to waive the fee in return for something of equal value, such as a twelve-month term.
options.B: Waive the fee straight away as a goodwill gesture, so the client feels looked after.
options.C: Promise a bigger discount on the call and get it approved by your manager afterwards.
options.D: Say "I'm sure we can do something" and work out the details after the call.

questions.stem:
A rep listens to her recorded calls. Every Acknowledge she uses is the same two words: "I understand."
What should she change?

options.A: Add "but" and a short explanation, so the acknowledgment leads somewhere useful.
options.B: Use a sentence she would actually say, such as "That's a fair worry."
options.C: Drop the acknowledgment and go straight to the reframe to save time on each call.
options.D: Say "I understand" twice, so it sounds warmer and more sincere to the client.

questions.stem:
You ran A.R.T. on a client's concern, and she says, "OK, that makes sense." You know her criteria, and the fit is clear.
What is the best next move?

options.A: "Great. Shall I send the contract over now?"
options.B: Keep reframing for another minute, to be sure the concern is fully gone.
options.C: Tell her the offer ends today, so she decides before the call ends.
options.D: Restate her criteria, show the evidence, name the consequence honestly, ask an open question, then offer two real dates.

questions.stem:
A client's current contract charges an exit fee if she leaves before March. It is January.
Which Consequence line is honest?

options.A: "Switching now means paying the exit fee. Waiting until March costs you nothing, so starting then may suit you better."
options.B: "Waiting is risky. Prices may go up next week, so it's better to switch today."
options.C: Skip the Consequence step, since mentioning the fee could lose the sale.
options.D: "Most of your neighbours have already switched, so waiting makes no sense."

questions.stem:
A call ends with the office manager saying, "We decide after the budget meeting on the 14th. Call me the next day at ten."
Which log entry is best?

options.A: "Interested. Call back."
options.B: "Office manager, positive call, good chance."
options.C: "Follow up after their meeting sometime next week."
options.D: "Spoke to Lina (office manager). Said: 'We decide after the budget meeting on the 14th.' Agreed: call on the 15th at 10:00."

questions.stem:
After fifteen fast "no"s in a row, a rep starts to feel the session is a failure and that the problem is her.
What does the course recommend?

options.A: Push harder on the next calls to make up for the ones she lost.
options.B: Treat each outcome as information and score herself on what she controls.
options.C: Stop logging the quick no's, so the session feels less discouraging.
options.D: Judge the session only by sales, since that is the number that really matters.

questions.stem:
In his second week in a new tele sales job, Ali wants to impress his manager. He plans to double his dials before learning the product or the rules on who may be called and when.
What should he do instead?

options.A: Double the dials anyway, because a high call count shows effort and effort is what counts.
options.B: Skip logging the short calls, so he has more time in each session to dial.
options.C: Learn the product and the contact rules first, keep his own call log, and watch conversations and conversion, not dials alone.
options.D: Extend his calls into the evening, when more people are home, to raise his contact rate.

questions.stem:
A new area manager writes down what she owns.
Which item is hers, not her unit managers'?

options.A: Which priorities matter across the area, and how her support is spread.
options.B: The daily decisions on each unit's pipeline and which quotes to chase first.
options.C: Each branch's customer relationships and who calls which client this week.
options.D: The daily behavior of each team on the sales floor and on the phones.

questions.stem:
An area manager wants all four units to open client calls with the same three-sentence script, and to reply to every new enquiry within the same set time.
What should become an area standard?

options.A: Both, because consistency across units always builds client trust.
options.B: Neither, because each unit manager knows their own clients best.
options.C: The response time, while the call opening stays with each unit.
options.D: The script, because the wording is what clients hear first on every call.

questions.stem:
On a call, a unit manager tells you, "Clients are unhappy everywhere this month." She bases it on one difficult conversation she had yesterday.
How should you treat it on your area map?

options.A: Rank her unit first for support straight away, since she raised the alarm.
options.B: As a lead to check against evidence, such as response times, missed promises and what clients said.
options.C: Ignore it completely, because one manager's feelings are not data.
options.D: Move most of your support to her unit until the mood there improves.

questions.stem:
One unit's conversion has slipped for two months. You are tempted to sit in on its pipeline review and phone the stalled clients yourself.
What is the best approach?

options.A: Phone the stalled clients yourself, since a senior voice reassures them and wins back time.
options.B: Set the unit a conversion push for next month, so the manager knows it is a priority.
options.C: Tell the manager how to close each stalled deal, since you have more selling experience.
options.D: Compare the slip with lead quality and cycle, take questions to the manager, and agree one action she owns.

questions.stem:
Unit North had 400 qualified opportunities and closed 80. Unit South had 100 and closed 30.
Which unit converted better?

options.A: North, because it closed far more sales over the period.
options.B: They converted equally well over the period.
options.C: Neither can be judged, because the units are different sizes.
options.D: South, at 30 percent against North's 20 percent.

questions.stem:
Before discussing any unit's performance, you use the course's fixed routine.
Which order is correct?

options.A: What changed, who is different, which behavior drives it, one thing to try.
options.B: Who is different, what changed, one thing to try, which behavior drives it.
options.C: Which behavior drives it, what changed, who is different, one thing to try.
options.D: One thing to try, what changed, which behavior drives it, who is different.

questions.stem:
After five steady months, one unit's conversion fell this month. A colleague says, "That manager has lost the plot."
What do you do first?

options.A: Call the manager and tell her the unit is now underperforming.
options.B: Set a recovery target for next month and review it then.
options.C: Set the drop beside lead quality, cycle, capacity and mix for the same periods.
options.D: Compare its closed totals with the largest unit in the area.

questions.stem:
Your comparison shows one unit's follow-up rate dropped from 85 to 55 percent in a month. You meet the unit manager.
What is the best opening?

options.A: "Your team has gone lazy on follow-up, and I need it fixed this month."
options.B: "Follow-up dropped from 85 to 55 percent. What changed? Pick one opportunity that went cold and walk me through it." Then wait.
options.C: "I'll sit with your reps this week and coach them on follow-up myself."
options.D: "Here are five things to fix: scripts, timing, CRM use, reminders and weekly checks."

questions.stem:
You observe a unit manager coaching a rep after a lost deal.
What should your feedback focus on?

options.A: The rep's selling mistakes, which you explain to the rep directly afterwards.
options.B: The manager's personality and general style as a leader of the team.
options.C: The manager's coaching behavior in that session.
options.D: The unit's conversion figures for the month so far.

questions.stem:
This morning you watched unit manager Lina coach a rep, Omar. Three times she finished his answers for him.
Which feedback follows SBI with the practice step?

options.A: "Lina, you are too controlling in your coaching sessions."
options.B: "Lina, in this morning's session you interrupted Omar three times. Try not to do that."
options.C: "Lina, you were impatient this morning, and Omar seemed unhappy."
options.D: "Lina, this morning you finished Omar's answers three times, and he stopped offering ideas. Let's rehearse letting him finish."

questions.stem:
A unit manager's coaching log shows nine sessions this month. Eight were with the same top rep.
What do you do?

options.A: Point to the pattern and ask how coaching will reach the rest of the team, with a dated check.
options.B: Praise the number of sessions, since nine is well above the area average.
options.C: Coach the other reps yourself, so nobody on the team is left behind.
options.D: Leave it alone, because the top rep's numbers went up this month.

questions.stem:
A unit manager tells you her lost deals are "all about price." The reps wrote "price" in the lost-sale notes, but the clients' own words say, "I didn't understand what was included." Other units do not show this.
What is your best move?

options.A: Approve a lower price for that unit, since the manager knows her clients best.
options.B: Read the clients' words with her, ask her to walk you through one lost deal, then agree one coaching change.
options.C: Accept the reps' summaries, since they were the ones on the calls.
options.D: Roll out new pricing materials to every unit in the area.

questions.stem:
Two responses could both fix a problem: a short shared product explanation, or a full redesign of all materials.
What should you do first?

options.A: The full redesign, because it covers everything at once.
options.B: The smaller response, tested first in a limited pilot.
options.C: Both at the same time, so the problem disappears faster.
options.D: Neither, until the problem appears in every single unit.

questions.stem:
Clients in four units say, "I couldn't tell which package was right for me." Each unit compares the offer to a different benchmark.
Which response fits?

options.A: Coach each manager separately on how their own team explains packages.
options.B: Ask every unit to make more calls this month to make up the gap.
options.C: Lower prices, so the choice feels less risky to the client.
options.D: One shared comparison guide that every unit uses.

questions.stem:
A month after rolling out a practice to three units, every manager tells you, "Yes, we're doing it."
What do you do next?

options.A: Check conversations, notes and observations for real use, against the measure set before the pilot.
options.B: Take their word for it, since they own execution in their units.
options.C: Wait for the quarter's results before looking at anything.
options.D: Roll it out to the remaining units straight away.

questions.stem:
Your two-unit pilot has ended. In one unit the success measure was met. In the other it was partly met, because the manager started two weeks late.
How does it go in your area review?

options.A: Report the unit that met the measure, and leave the other out to keep the story clear.
options.B: Announce an area-wide rollout now, since the pilot has proved that it works.
options.C: Mark one done and one partial with the reason, and recommend the next step with a date.
options.D: Leave the pilot out of the review until both units have complete results.

questions.stem:
Your draft area review is nine pages of unit-by-unit detail.
What should it contain instead?

options.A: All nine pages, so the leader has every fact available.
options.B: One line: "Sales are down, we are working on it."
options.C: A story of the month's main client conversations.
options.D: Results against target with context, customer-facing risks, and decisions needed.

questions.stem:
You hold a quarterly area review and send nothing in between. Your senior leader has started skipping your updates.
What does the course recommend?

options.A: Wait for the next review and make it longer and more detailed.
options.B: A short written summary after each review, updates at an agreed interval, and a note when a commitment closes.
options.C: A long daily report covering every unit in the area.
options.D: Contact the leader only when there is bad news to share.

questions.stem:
Your unit managers report twelve client concerns this month.
Which belong in your review to senior leaders?

options.A: All twelve, so that nothing important is missed.
options.B: None, because client concerns belong to unit managers.
options.C: Only those that would change a senior leader's decision.
options.D: The ones raised by the loudest or most senior clients.

questions.stem:
A key account shared by two units complains that each unit gives a different turnaround time for repairs. Fixing it needs a senior decision on one area-wide repair promise. The account manager in one unit leads the client relationship.
What do you do?

options.A: In the review, name the risk with evidence from both units, note that the account manager leads the client, and recommend one standard with a decision date.
options.B: Call the client yourself and promise one turnaround time, then tell the two managers.
options.C: Send senior leaders every unit's repair figures and let them draw their own conclusions.
options.D: Ask senior leaders in the review, "What should we do about repair times?"

questions.stem:
On her first Monday as sales manager, Hana sits down to plan the week.
Which question should she start with?

options.A: "What do I need to close personally this week to hit my number?"
options.B: "Where should our selling effort go this cycle, and what will it cost?"
options.C: "Which accounts called me most last week, so I can get back to them first?"
options.D: "Which of the biggest deals can I take over myself to make sure they land?"

questions.stem:
The business objective is growth this year. Segment one, hospitals, is large, but you have no references there and buying runs through nine-month tenders. Segment two, small clinics, is smaller, but your team already has 30 relationships there and clinics buy direct.
Which should be the priority this cycle?

options.A: Hospitals, because the bigger market is the bigger forecast.
options.B: Both equally, so no opportunity is missed this year.
options.C: Neither, until the team has sold in both for a full year.
options.D: Clinics, because the team can serve them well now.

questions.stem:
A draft priority plan says, "We will stop field visits to our smallest accounts this cycle." Nothing else is written about those accounts.
What is missing?

options.A: How those accounts will be served instead, such as inside support or a partner.
options.B: Nothing, because the not-pursued line is already the hardest part to write.
options.C: A promise to keep visiting them now and then, so nobody notices the change.
options.D: A few more priorities, so the plan looks as ambitious as the business wants.

questions.stem:
Your plan frees two reps from core accounts to work a new segment. When you allocate the target, the core channel's slice is still the same as last year.
What should you do?

options.A: Keep the core slice as it is and expect the remaining reps to cover the freed reps' accounts too.
options.B: Raise the new segment's slice until the totals match, because the business needs the growth.
options.C: Lower the core slice for the capacity moved, write the trade-off beside it, and raise any gap in the total openly.
options.D: Quietly drop the new segment if it falls behind, so the core slice can still be met.

questions.stem:
You are setting next year's target for one channel.
Which is the right base to start from?

options.A: What it actually delivered over the last few comparable periods.
options.B: Its single best month this year, multiplied by twelve.
options.C: Last year's total plus a growth percentage that sounds inspiring.
options.D: The growth rate your main competitor announced this year.

questions.stem:
A company sells through distributors and through a direct key-account team. The new manager splits the target equally across four regions, because that is how the org chart is drawn.
What does the course say?

options.A: Keep the regional split, since equal slices feel fair to every team.
options.B: Split it evenly by rep headcount, so every person carries the same number.
options.C: Split by channel first, then by territory inside each channel.
options.D: Keep one shared number for the whole team, so everyone owns all of it.

questions.stem:
A manager's allocation adds exactly 10 percent to each channel's slice from last year. The total is last year's plus 10 percent.
What check does the course ask for?

options.A: None, because a proportional increase is the fairest split there is.
options.B: Build the allocation bottom-up from channel evidence and capacity, then compare.
options.C: Raise the strongest channel's slice further, to build in a safety margin.
options.D: Leave it, and let the review points correct any slice that turns out wrong.

questions.stem:
At the planned mid-year review point, the partner channel is 30 percent ahead of its slice. Most of the gain comes from one large order. A team lead proposes moving part of the direct target onto partners for the rest of the year.
What do you do?

options.A: Agree now, since the partner channel has clearly outgrown its slice.
options.B: Raise the partner slice and keep direct unchanged, so the total rises.
options.C: Change nothing, and wait for the year-end result before looking again.
options.D: Strip out the one-off order, check the written partner assumption, then decide what the review may change.

questions.stem:
Calls made dropped sharply this month, but closed deals are on plan.
What is the most likely reading?

options.A: There is no problem, because the outcome numbers are steady.
options.B: Activity does not matter, because outcomes held without it.
options.C: The team must have changed size, so the averages moved.
options.D: A lag effect: the drop may show up in closed deals later.

questions.stem:
Your pipeline shows few deals at first contact, and fourteen deals that have sat in negotiation for more than three months.
How should you read it?

options.A: As a warning: deals sitting still late in the pipeline may not be real deals.
options.B: As a healthy pipeline, since a full late stage means a strong quarter is coming.
options.C: As a problem at first contact only, because the early stage is too thin.
options.D: As forecast-ready, so add all fourteen to the forecast at full value.

questions.stem:
The team closed its target number of deals this quarter, but revenue is 15 percent below plan. The average deal value fell.
What kind of gap is this?

options.A: A volume gap, so the fix is more calls and more meetings this quarter.
options.B: A conversion gap, so the fix is in how quotes are handled.
options.C: A price gap: deals are closing, but at a lower value than planned.
options.D: No real gap, so lower the revenue target quietly to match the deals.

questions.stem:
One rep's win rate on quotes fell from one in two to one in four. You check the lost quotes: most went out on an old price list, because the new list was never added to the quote templates his branch uses.
What is the gap, and what is the fix?

options.A: A skill gap: role-play quote handling with the rep this week.
options.B: A process gap: get the templates updated, with an owner and a date.
options.C: A capacity gap: move some of the rep's accounts to a colleague.
options.D: A volume gap: ask the rep to send more quotes to make up the difference.

questions.stem:
Before sending a quote, a rep confirmed the client's delivery date, and the client signed the same day.
Which feedback best helps the rep repeat it?

options.A: "Great job on that one!"
options.B: "You're a natural closer. Keep it up."
options.C: "In Tuesday's quote, you confirmed the delivery date before sending, and the client signed that day. Keep doing that."
options.D: Say nothing, because coaching time is for fixing mistakes.

questions.stem:
You are about to join a rep on a client visit for the first time.
What do you tell the rep before you go in?

options.A: "I'm here to check on how you are doing."
options.B: "I'm here to see what works, so we can build on it."
options.C: "If it starts going wrong, I'll take over the meeting."
options.D: Nothing. The rep will see why you are there.

questions.stem:
You asked a rep to "review every key account by month-end." He phoned each one. You meant a full account review with the client, as the team had done before.
What kind of gap is this, and what fixes it?

options.A: A skill gap, fixed with a role-play on running account reviews.
options.B: Persistent underperformance, fixed with a formal conversation.
options.C: A capacity gap, fixed by moving some accounts to a colleague.
options.D: An expectation gap, fixed with a written standard he can repeat back.

questions.stem:
Last week a rep committed in the review to send a revised proposal with phased payments by Friday. The tracker shows it was sent on time. The client is still silent.
What do you do in this week's review?

options.A: Mark it done, then ask whether it worked. If payment terms were not the blocker, find what is before agreeing the next action.
options.B: Mark it done and move on, since the commitment was kept.
options.C: Tell the rep to try harder with the client, since the deal still has not moved.
options.D: Add five new commitments for this deal, so nothing is left untried.

questions.stem:
Leadership asks whether a strategic account will close this quarter. You honestly do not know yet.
What do you say?

options.A: "Yes, it will close," because a decisive answer builds confidence.
options.B: "We will have to wait and see how it goes."
options.C: Give a high figure and pad it a little, so it sounds safe.
options.D: "I don't know yet. We will have a clear answer by the last Friday of the month."

questions.stem:
You have three candidate actions for the next 30 days. Action X would close half the gap, but you are 20 percent confident it will work. Action Y would close a fifth of the gap, at 80 percent confidence. Action Z would close 30 percent of the gap, at 40 percent confidence.
Which do you run first?

options.A: Action X, because it addresses the largest share of the gap.
options.B: Action Y, because it has the largest expected impact.
options.C: Action Z, because it sits in the middle on both measures.
options.D: All three at once, so the gap closes as fast as possible.

questions.stem:
Your 30-day plan aims to cut quote turnaround time. Every faster quote still needs a pricing approval from finance.
When do you involve finance?

options.A: Name the person in finance and walk them through the plan before it starts.
options.B: After the first week, once you have results to show them.
options.C: Only if the plan fails and approvals turn out to be the cause.
options.D: Let each rep contact finance individually when they need an approval.

questions.stem:
Your new segment priority rests on a conversion rate of one in four account reviews. You have never tested that rate. Leadership asks for next quarter's forecast for the segment.
What do you report?

options.A: Present the figure as firm, since leaders prefer confident numbers they can plan with.
options.B: Leave the segment out of the forecast entirely until your own records exist.
options.C: The number and your confidence, the conversion rate labeled as an untested assumption, and what would change the outcome.
options.D: Use the largest market figure you can find, so the segment looks worth the investment.

questions.stem: Which list gives the three steps of A.I.M. in the correct order?

options.A: Acknowledge, Illuminate, Mobilize
options.B: Anchor, Mobilize, Illuminate
options.C: Anchor, Illuminate, Mobilize
options.D: Anchor, Inform, Move

questions.stem: A customer quotes specifications from memory and steps back each time you move closer. Which decision style is this, and what do you do?

options.A: Wants you to lead: give one clear recommendation with one reason, then guide the next step
options.B: Careful and anxious: slow down and reassure them about the return policy before anything else
options.C: Ready to buy: skip the questions and take the item straight to the till for them
options.D: Wants facts and room: give accurate information, then pause and let them think

questions.stem: A customer walks in fast, phone in hand, and heads straight for the shelving aisle. Which opener follows the First-Contact Standard?

options.A: "Hi, can I help you find something today? We have a few offers on shelving this week."
options.B: "Hi, I work here. Take your time, I'm close by. You went straight for the shelving; what space is it for?"
options.C: "Hi there! Our best-selling shelving unit is just over here. Let me show you why everyone is buying it."
options.D: "Hi, are you looking for shelving? Would you like me to walk you through the whole range?"

questions.stem: Two associates on the same shift are both polite and know the products. Which behavior marks the strong associate?

options.A: They end every contact with a next step that has a date in it
options.B: They answer every question fully and repeat the features when the customer hesitates
options.C: They wait for the customer to ask a question, so they never seem pushy
options.D: They say "No problem" to "I'll think about it" and move quickly to the next person

questions.stem: In one week your 20 sales contained 30 items in total. Which of your four numbers is 1.5?

options.A: Conversion
options.B: Average sale
options.C: Add-on rate
options.D: Units per sale

questions.stem: Your conversion has fallen three weeks in a row while your other numbers stayed flat. Since a new stock layout arrived, you spend the start of each shift restocking. What is the most useful conclusion?

options.A: The floor has been quiet, so the number will recover on its own in a week or two
options.B: A behavior changed: you are greeting customers late, often after they have passed your section
options.C: The new stock layout is the real problem, so you should wait for your manager to change it back
options.D: You need to push harder on every customer you speak with until the number recovers

questions.stem: Your add-on rate is your weakest number. You notice you always mention the service plan at the till, after the customer has paid. What one change does the course suggest?

options.A: Mention the service plan as soon as the customer walks in, so they know it exists
options.B: Mention the service plan to every customer twice, once early and once at the till
options.C: After the customer says yes to the main item, explain the plan in two sentences before payment
options.D: Change your greeting, your discovery questions and your add-on timing all in the same week

questions.stem: Which line belongs in your daily record?

options.A: "Customer buying a gift for a teenager; returning Thursday for the smaller size."
options.B: "Mrs. K. (phone number noted) might come back at some point for the smaller size."
options.C: "Busy day, lots of people in, felt like it went well overall on the floor."
options.D: "Spoke to a customer about a gift; told them to come back whenever suits them."

questions.stem: Three customers are waiting while you serve one at the till. What is the strongest move?

options.A: Speed up the till customer so the queue clears faster for everyone waiting
options.B: Keep your eyes on the till customer until you are free, then greet the whole queue together
options.C: Give the next waiting customer a two-second acknowledgment, then return fully to the till
options.D: Ask the waiting customers to come back later, when the floor is less busy

questions.stem: You are with a customer, and another one is waiting. Which line is the honest respect-for-time line?

options.A: "I'm with someone just now; I'll be with you in a few minutes, or have a look around first."
options.B: "Two minutes, I promise. I'm nearly done here, so please just wait right there for me."
options.C: "I'll be with you in exactly five minutes, so you won't have to wait any longer than that."
options.D: "Someone will be with you eventually; it's very busy today, so please bear with us."

questions.stem: A customer you served last week comes back and stops at the same product. Which second approach is strongest?

options.A: "Welcome back! How can I help you today? Let me know if you need anything at all."
options.B: "Good to see you again. The larger size you looked at is back in stock. What made you come back to it?"
options.C: Say nothing and let them browse, because they will ask if they need you this time
options.D: "Welcome back! Since you're a returning customer, I can take a little something off the price today."

questions.stem: A couple walks in to look at a sofa. One keeps testing the cushions; the other keeps checking the label. What is the best single question?

options.A: "Who will be making the final decision on this today?"
options.B: "What matters most to each of you on this?"
options.C: "Can I show you our best-selling sofa first?"
options.D: "Why are you replacing your current sofa?"

questions.stem: A customer says she has read every review of a backpack and knows she wants the 40-liter model. What is the best first question?

options.A: "What is the one thing the reviews didn't settle for you?"
options.B: "Did you know the 40-liter model is our best seller this month?"
options.C: "Reviews are often unreliable. Shall I show you the other sizes?"
options.D: "Why did you decide on the 40-liter one rather than the bigger one?"

questions.stem: A customer says, "I know exactly what I want," and names a coffee machine a friend owns. What do you do?

options.A: Tell them their friend's model is a poor choice and show them a better one
options.B: Show them several other machines at once, so they can see the full range
options.C: Hand them the box straight away and say nothing more about it, out of respect for their plan
options.D: Confirm their choice, then ask one follow-up such as "What will you use it for most often?"

questions.stem: A nervous customer is buying a gift for a colleague and has no idea what to choose. Which question fits best?

options.A: "Roughly what budget did you have in mind for the gift?"
options.B: "Do you want the most popular option we have for colleagues?"
options.C: "Tell me a bit about the person you're buying for. What are they into?"
options.D: "Why did you leave the gift so late?"

questions.stem: You have asked a customer what they are shopping for, who it is for and what their budget is. What should you ask next?

options.A: "Great, let me show you our best model for that budget straight away."
options.B: "Which color would you like it in, black or silver?"
options.C: "Would you like to see it in the box or on display?"
options.D: "What has made this hard to choose so far?"

questions.stem: A customer told you their last vacuum was too heavy to carry up the stairs. Which line is a benefit tied to their stated need?

options.A: "This model has lightweight construction and a high-grade motor."
options.B: "This is our best-selling model, so it is a very safe choice for you."
options.C: "This one is light enough for you to carry up the stairs."
options.D: "This model is lighter than most vacuums on the market today."

questions.stem: You have anchored on the customer's need: a bag that survives a commute and fits a laptop. What does the Illuminate step look like?

options.A: Show one thing that removes that need, with proof they can check, such as the laptop sleeve to test
options.B: List every feature of the bag, so the customer can see the full value of what they are buying
options.C: Ask the customer to tell you again what they need, so you are sure you heard them right
options.D: Tell the customer the bag is very popular with commuters and that they will not regret it

questions.stem: A customer shows you a lower online price for the same model. What do you say first?

options.A: "Online sellers won't help you if something goes wrong, so I would be careful there."
options.B: "That seller might not even be real. A lot of those listings are not what they seem."
options.C: "I can't match that, so it's up to you whether you buy it here or online today."
options.D: "That's a fair price, and it's worth comparing. Here's what we can confirm today."

questions.stem: Five sweaters fit what the customer described. What does the course tell you to do?

options.A: Show all five, so the customer has the widest possible choice
options.B: Narrow to two, and name the one difference that matters for their stated need
options.C: Show only the one you prefer, so the decision is quick and easy for them
options.D: Let the customer browse all five alone, so they do not feel any pressure

questions.stem: A customer says, "I'll think about it," and has asked you twice how the return process works. Which source of objection is most likely underneath?

options.A: Price
options.B: Need
options.C: Timing
options.D: Trust

questions.stem: A customer says, "I'll just buy it online." You have acknowledged the feeling. Which line is the Reframe step of A.R.T.?

options.A: "Our product is much better quality than anything you'll find online, so it's worth paying a bit more."
options.B: "Buying in person means no wait, no return trip and someone to set it up. What's that worth to you?"
options.C: "Would you like me to match the online price, so you can take it home today instead?"
options.D: "Online sellers often send damaged items, so you would be taking a real risk there."

questions.stem: A customer asks for a discount. A small one is possible within policy. What do you say?

options.A: "I can look at what's possible if we settle on the size today. How does that sound?"
options.B: "Of course. I'll take ten percent off now, so you don't have to think about it any more."
options.C: "I can do even better than that. Let me take fifteen percent off for you right now."
options.D: "This price ends tonight, so a discount isn't needed. You should really buy it today."

questions.stem: You offered the discount only in exchange for a decision today. The customer pushes a second time for the discount with no decision. What do you do?

options.A: Give the discount now to end the discomfort, because repeating the request shows they are serious
options.B: Explain the store's pricing policy in full detail, so the customer understands every reason
options.C: Restate the trade once, calmly, then ask, "What would need to happen for today to work?"
options.D: Tell the customer that asking twice is rude, and that the original price will now stand

questions.stem: When is the best moment to suggest an add-on?

options.A: While the customer is still comparing the main options, so they see the full cost
options.B: After the customer has committed to the main item
options.C: As the customer walks in, so they know the whole range before they start
options.D: At the till after payment, because it is the last chance before they leave

questions.stem: You are about to suggest a carry case with a camera. Which question do you ask yourself first?

options.A: Would I recommend it if I earned nothing from it?
options.B: Is it the most expensive case we have in stock?
options.C: Can the customer afford it on top of the camera?
options.D: Has my manager asked for more add-ons this week?

questions.stem: A customer asks about an extended plan for a phone. Which explanation follows the course's rules?

options.A: "You'll want this. Phones like this one tend to break, so the plan really pays for itself."
options.B: "This plan is required with this phone, so I'll add it to the total for you now."
options.C: "It covers everything that could happen to the phone, so you'll never pay for a repair."
options.D: "It covers mechanical failure. It doesn't cover accidental damage, such as a cracked screen."

questions.stem: A customer declines the add-on you suggested. What do you do next?

options.A: Suggest a second, cheaper add-on, so they leave with at least one extra item
options.B: Ask once more, in case they did not understand how useful the add-on would be
options.C: Accept the no completely and move on to the next step of the sale
options.D: Explain what could go wrong without the add-on, then ask them again

questions.stem: A customer has explained what a fridge must do and is ready to choose a delivery date. You have not checked whether that model is in stock for delivery. Which of the 5 conditions before closing is not yet met?

options.A: The evidence is verified and shared
options.B: The customer's criteria are clear in their own words
options.C: The decision-maker is present or included
options.D: The consequences are honest

questions.stem: All 5 conditions are met for a high-value purchase. Which question fits the Commitment Close?

options.A: "So, shall we go ahead with this one today?"
options.B: "Would you like me to write it up for you?"
options.C: "What would you need to see to start on the 15th?"
options.D: "Can I take your number and follow up later?"

questions.stem: A customer wants a sofa, but their partner decides and has not seen it. What do you do?

options.A: Encourage them to decide now and talk it over with their partner at home tonight
options.B: Ask what the partner will want to know, give it plainly, and agree a dated next step
options.C: Offer an extra discount if they decide today, before the partner has a chance to object
options.D: Say nothing more and wait for them to come back on their own with the partner

questions.stem: A customer wants to think about a coat, and your store's policy allows a hold. What makes the hold honest?

options.A: Telling the customer the coat will be gone today if they do not take the hold
options.B: Promising that the price will stay the same for as long as they need to decide
options.C: Keeping the coat aside without telling them when the hold ends, so they feel no pressure
options.D: Stating the date the hold ends and what it does not guarantee, then agreeing a follow-up

questions.stem: A customer puts a pair of boots on the counter: "These fell apart in three weeks." You have acknowledged the feeling. Which line is the Reframe?

options.A: "I check the receipt and the sole first so the refund clears on your card today, not after a warehouse decision."
options.B: "These boots are usually very strong. Most customers never have any problems with them at all."
options.C: "Our policy says we need to inspect every single item first, so there is nothing I can do about that part, sorry."
options.D: "Would you like a refund? If so, I'll need to see the receipt and check the sole first."

questions.stem: A customer leaves a laptop for repair. Which handover is clear and honest?

options.A: "It'll be ready soon, don't worry. We'll give you a call as soon as it's back with us."
options.B: "The repair takes three to five working days. Bring this slip, and here's the number if anything changes."
options.C: "The workshop will sort it all out for you, and someone from their team will be in touch with you directly."
options.D: "I'll make sure it's back by Friday, I promise. Just come in on Friday and it'll be ready."

questions.stem: A customer's size is out of stock. You want to keep one small promise. Which promise do you make?

options.A: "Your size will definitely be back on Monday, so come in then and it will be here."
options.B: "I'll make sure the warehouse sends your size to this store first, ahead of everyone."
options.C: "I'll check the restock and message you when your size lands, as you said you'd like."
options.D: "I'll put one aside for you from the next delivery, whatever happens with the stock."

questions.stem: You want to let repeat customers know when items they asked about come back in. Which approach is honest and within policy?

options.A: Add every customer who buys something to a contact list and send them a message each week
options.B: Message customers whenever there is a promotion, since they shopped with you before
options.C: Ask permission, note the answer honestly, and only contact those who agreed, inside policy
options.D: Contact customers only when you need to hit your weekly numbers, so it stays occasional

questions.stem: You know a mystery shopper may visit this week. Which behavior most reliably scores well?

options.A: Extra product detail at every step, to show your expertise
options.B: A more formal script than usual, so nothing is missed
options.C: A faster close on every contact, to keep the queue moving
options.D: The same calm, interested contact you give every customer

questions.stem: You are two weeks into a sales slump. What is the strongest first move?

options.A: Push harder and talk faster with every customer, to force more sales out of the quiet floor
options.B: Set the goal "sell more this week" and keep it in mind on every shift until the dip ends
options.C: Wait for the floor to get busier, because a slump is usually caused by a lack of customers
options.D: Pick one controllable behavior, such as one more discovery question per customer, for five shifts

questions.stem: Your shift is ending, and you pass a customer to a colleague. What do you do?

options.A: Tell your colleague what the customer is looking for and what is decided, introduce them by role, and step back
options.B: Tell the customer that a colleague will help them now, and let them explain everything again from the beginning
options.C: Stay with the customer after your shift ends, so no colleague ever has to take over your customers
options.D: Ask the customer to come back tomorrow, when you are on shift again and can finish what you started

questions.stem: You are building your promotion case. Which statement is the stronger argument to bring to your manager?

options.A: "My conversion is good. I think I'm one of the best sellers on the floor."
options.B: "My conversion has climbed over six weeks, and here is the behavior I changed."
options.C: "I've been here longer than most people, so I think it's my turn for promotion."
options.D: "Everyone likes working with me, and customers often say I'm very friendly."

questions.stem: Which list gives the four behaviors of the First-Contact Standard in the order this course teaches?

options.A: Relevance, Low Threat, Curiosity, Autonomy
options.B: Low Threat, Autonomy, Relevance, Curiosity
options.C: Low Threat, Relevance, Curiosity, Autonomy
options.D: Curiosity, Relevance, Autonomy, Low Threat

questions.stem: A customer in work clothes steps up to a parts counter early in the morning. Which opening follows the First-Contact Standard?

options.A: "Morning. The pump on that shelf is our most popular one, it's four hundred. Do you want me to get it down for you?"
options.B: "Morning! You'll want our new range, everyone is buying it this week. What sort of budget are you working with today?"
options.C: "Morning, I work this counter. If now's not a good time, someone can help you later. Most people in this early need something for a job today. What are you working on?"
options.D: "Morning. Are you actually going to buy something today, or are you just having a look around the counter?"

questions.stem: A customer says the sealed unit costs too much. You have acknowledged the feeling and reframed. Which question is a correct Transition in A.R.T.?

options.A: "Do you want the cheaper unit instead of this one?"
options.B: "If I take something off, will you take it today?"
options.C: "Shall I go ahead and order it for you now, so it's here for the job?"
options.D: "What would need to be true for this to work for your job?"

questions.stem: The course says good counter work has three visible parts. Which three?

options.A: Keeping the queue short, answering every phone call, and keeping the counter tidy all day
options.B: How fast you serve, how well you know the stock, and how pleasant you are with customers
options.C: How a contact opens, how a concern is handled, and how a decision is reached
options.D: Greeting each customer, offering an extra item to everyone, and taking the payment quickly

questions.stem: This week your sales total went up, but only because you served more customers; the average value per customer is still below last month's. What does the course say this shows?

options.A: Every customer should be pushed harder to spend more before they reach the till
options.B: Nothing is wrong, because the total went up and that is the figure that matters most
options.C: The total is fine, so the average per customer can be left until the monthly review
options.D: A drift: each customer is buying less, and the higher total is hiding it

questions.stem: You are not sure which of your counter figures your employer actually sets a target on. What does the course suggest?

options.A: Assume every figure counts and give all of them equal effort until someone tells you otherwise
options.B: Set your own targets for the figures you think ought to exist, so you have something to aim at
options.C: Ask your supervisor what being on track would look like, then write a one-page target card from the answer
options.D: Wait until the next review to find out which figures were scored, then adjust your work from there week by week

questions.stem: Your returns rose this month and your manager asks about it. Which reply follows the course's four moves for explaining a missed number?

options.A: "My returns rose this month. Most came from parts sold without checking the fit with the customer. This week I'm checking the fit before every sale. What would you need to see next week to tell me it's working?"
options.B: "The whole team's returns were up this month, not only mine, so I don't think it's really about how I serve customers."
options.C: "It was a really difficult month with the queue and the phones, but I promise I'll try harder and do better next month."
options.D: "Customers just returned more this month. It happens sometimes, and there isn't much anyone at the counter can do about it."

questions.stem: Why does the course tell you to read your figures in a series rather than one day at a time?

options.A: A series looks better to your manager than a single bad day on its own
options.B: Employers only ever score weekly figures, so the daily ones are not worth reading or recording at all
options.C: Daily figures are usually wrong, so only the weekly totals can be trusted
options.D: One slow day is weather; several slow days in a row is a pattern with a cause you can look for

questions.stem: A customer says, "I want to speak to your manager." According to the course, what is this request often about?

options.A: A sign that the customer is trying to get something from the store that they are not entitled to
options.B: A signal that the matter is over and you should stop talking to the customer
options.C: Proof that you handled the matter badly and should now step aside from it
options.D: Respect: the customer wants to know someone with more authority has heard them

questions.stem: A customer's part does not fit, though it matches what was ordered. The customer has lost time on a job and asks for your manager. Which Reframe fits A.R.T.?

options.A: "I can't change what was ordered, and stepping back: what will cost you most is another day without the machine running."
options.B: "The order clearly says this part, so the sale itself was correct."
options.C: "Our returns policy is clear, so let me explain it again for you."
options.D: "My manager will only tell you the same thing that I am telling you."

questions.stem: A customer is getting loud at the counter while the queue watches. What does the course suggest you do with your own voice?

options.A: Speed it up, so that the conversation ends as quickly as it possibly can
options.B: Raise it to match the customer, so that everyone can hear you clearly
options.C: Stop speaking and turn away from the customer until they have calmed down
options.D: Keep it at its normal level, or lower it slightly, and stay unhurried

questions.stem: You are passing an escalated complaint to your manager. Which four things does the course say the handover note should contain?

options.A: The time, the queue length, which colleague was nearby, and what the customer bought
options.B: What the customer asked for, what you said, what happened next, and what you recommend
options.C: The customer's name, phone number, home address and the full wording of the complaint as they said it
options.D: Your opinion of the customer, who was to blame, the policy, and how you felt about it

questions.stem: A customer brings back a tool set eleven days past the return window, with no receipt. What is the strongest first move?

options.A: Pause, then name the feeling and ask one open question to hear what sits under the request
options.B: Call your manager over before saying anything at all to the customer about the return
options.C: Give a full refund at once, because a return dispute is never worth the conflict it causes
options.D: Quote the policy rule straight away, so the customer knows exactly where the store stands

questions.stem: A trade customer asks for a payment delay on the account. You are not authorized to approve credit decisions. What should you do?

options.A: Say "maybe" and hope the customer does not bring it up again before paying
options.B: Say plainly where the decision sits, then keep the customer with you while it is reviewed
options.C: Tell the customer credit is not possible here, so the matter is closed quickly and nobody is kept waiting
options.D: Approve a short delay yourself, since a small amount keeps the customer happy

questions.stem: Why does a refusal said as a command, such as "No, that's against policy," often make a customer push back harder?

options.A: Store policies are too complicated for most customers to follow or accept
options.B: The customer feels their freedom to choose is squeezed, so they push back or leave
options.C: Customers always want to speak to a manager, whatever the counter tells them
options.D: Most customers expect a refund whenever they bring an item back, whatever the condition of the item

questions.stem: You must refuse a request that sits outside policy. How does the course say to deliver the refusal?

options.A: A firm reminder that the customer should have checked the conditions when they bought it
options.B: A quick no with no further detail, so the queue can keep moving and nobody argues
options.C: One clear sentence, what the customer can still do, including escalating, then one open question
options.D: A full explanation of the rule and its history, so the customer understands why it exists and accepts it

questions.stem: A customer looks at your quote and says, "That's too dear." Why does the course tell you to take the Mandatory Pause before you answer?

options.A: So you have a few seconds to work out the biggest discount you are allowed to give the customer
options.B: So the customer understands, without being told, that the price is not negotiable
options.C: So the silence makes the customer uncomfortable enough to accept the price as it is
options.D: So you answer the doubt behind the number instead of defending the price or cutting it

questions.stem: Which Acknowledge line fits A.R.T. as this course teaches it?

options.A: "It sounds like you expected this to come in lower."
options.B: "I can see the price surprised you. Let me knock a bit off for you."
options.C: "I can hear you expected it lower, and that's completely fair."
options.D: "It sounds like a lot to spend today, but the quality justifies it."

questions.stem: A trade customer hears your quote and says, "I can get that for 190 down the road." Which pushback is this, and what does the course say to do?

options.A: Price shock: list every feature of your product until the number starts to make sense to the customer
options.B: A discount habit: knock some money off now so that the customer keeps coming back to you every month
options.C: A lost sale: match the 190 straight away, because the customer has already decided to buy elsewhere
options.D: A quoted cheaper price: ask how the other quote was built and what it covers, then reframe to its gaps

questions.stem: A trade customer says a pack of sealing fittings is too dear for the job. Which Reframe fits A.R.T.?

options.A: "Our fittings are the best brand we stock, and they have more features than anything else on the shelf."
options.B: "If a seal fails on site, you're back on the road for a return visit, and that's your afternoon gone."
options.C: "Every other trade customer pays this price for these fittings without ever raising it as a concern."
options.D: "The shop down the road sells poor quality fittings, so I really wouldn't buy anything from them."

questions.stem: A customer needs forty boxes of floor tiles for a job starting Monday. The stock screen shows thirty-eight. What is the stronger move?

options.A: Tell the customer you have about forty and they can collect them on Monday morning
options.B: Promise the full forty now and sort out the two missing boxes with the warehouse later
options.C: Tell the customer the stock system is often wrong, so they may want to try elsewhere
options.D: Tell the customer what the screen shows, confirm the gap with the warehouse, and give the true position before they leave

questions.stem: A special order promised for Tuesday has not arrived by Thursday, and you call purchasing. Which opening fits the course?

options.A: "It sounds like this order has been stuck somewhere. The customer was told Tuesday. What do you need from me to get a real date on this today?"
options.B: "You promised this order for Tuesday and it's now Thursday. What on earth is going on back there with it?"
options.C: "Can you please just hurry this order up for me? The customer is getting impatient at the counter."
options.D: "This is the third late order this month, and I'm the one who has to explain it to every customer."

questions.stem: Which sentence names the owner of a customer problem most clearly?

options.A: "The warehouse is dealing with it now, so the customer should hear something from someone soon enough."
options.B: "I'll get someone to look into it for the customer as soon as they have a moment."
options.C: "It should all be sorted out soon, so there is nothing more anyone needs to do."
options.D: "I'll take this to the customer. Can you confirm the stock position by this afternoon?"

questions.stem: A trade order is short by one box, and the customer is at the counter. You have asked the warehouse to bring it up. What do you say to the customer?

options.A: "I've spoken to the warehouse and the box is being brought up. While we wait, what else does the crew need?"
options.B: "It's not my fault, to be honest. The warehouse packed this order, so they are the ones who got it wrong."
options.C: "This happens a lot, unfortunately. The warehouse gets orders wrong quite often, so it's worth checking."
options.D: "Sorry about this, the warehouse is being really slow again today, as it often is on busy mornings."

questions.stem: In a closing review of a lost sale, you see that you knew what the job needed, in the customer's words, but you listed the premium line's features without matching them to it. Which step of the Commitment Close fell apart?

options.A: Calibrated question
options.B: Evidence
options.C: Genuine choice
options.D: Consequence

questions.stem: Your accuracy check shows four corrections in one busy Saturday shift, all of them quantity errors. What is the best move?

options.A: Stop taking orders during busy shifts and ask customers to come back another day
options.B: Skip the read-back on Saturdays so that the queue moves faster and nobody waits long
options.C: Add a short read-back before payment that you can use even when there is a queue
options.D: Accept that Saturday shifts are simply error-prone and nothing can be done about it

questions.stem: Your manager will observe your counter work in two days. Which preparation does the course recommend?

options.A: Write down three things you want to show, rehearse the weakest aloud, and prepare one sentence on what you are working on
options.B: Swap your shift with a colleague so that the observation happens on another day
options.C: Plan to talk faster on the day, so that you can show more in the time available
options.D: Rehearse every possible sentence you might say to each kind of customer, word for word, so that nothing at all can go wrong on the day

questions.stem: A colleague matched a competitor's lower price the moment a customer mentioned it. Which feedback follows the shape the course teaches?

options.A: "I noticed you matched the other price straight away. It seemed to close the question fast. What's your read on it?"
options.B: "Do you agree that you got that one wrong? I think most of the team would have handled it very differently."
options.C: "You were great with that customer today. Honestly, keep doing exactly what you are doing at the counter."
options.D: "You should never match a price that quickly. Always check what the customer needs before you do anything."

questions.stem: Three people are waiting while you serve a customer. How does the course say to acknowledge the queue?

options.A: Speed up and skip the smaller steps with the customer in front, so the queue clears faster and nobody has to wait for very long at all
options.B: Give the next person one short line with a true estimate, then return your full attention to the customer in front
options.C: Tell everyone in the queue that it shouldn't be long, whatever the real wait is likely to be
options.D: Keep chatting to the people in the queue while you serve, so that nobody feels left out

questions.stem: The phone rings while the counter is full and you are mid-order. Which response does the course recommend to the caller?

options.A: "Would you like me to call you back at some point later on this afternoon, when it is a bit quieter here at the counter?"
options.B: "Can you call back later? We're really busy right now." Then end the call quickly
options.C: "It's busy at the counter. I can take your order now, or call you back in ten minutes. What suits you better?"
options.D: Say "Hang on" to the customer at the counter and take the call while everyone waits

questions.stem: A customer's part needs checking in the back. Which line says the wait plainly, as the course teaches?

options.A: "It shouldn't be long at all, so just bear with me for a little while if you don't mind waiting."
options.B: "Two minutes, tops," when you know from experience that a check in the back takes much longer.
options.C: "Checking a part in the back takes about ten minutes. I'll go now and come back with an answer."
options.D: "I'm not really sure how long it will be. It depends on how things are going back there today."

questions.stem: Your shift ends with a customer's order half done. What does a clean handover include?

options.A: The part number written on a note left on the desk for whoever comes in next
options.B: What the customer needs, what is done and what is next, then telling the customer who takes over and when
options.C: A quick wave to the colleague taking over, so the customer can explain it to them again
options.D: A text message to the customer after you leave, explaining that someone else will now pick up their order from where you stopped

questions.stem: A regular fitter asks for a ten-unit discount per part on a fifty-part order. Your employer lets you approve up to five. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Refuse any discount at all, so that the fitter stops asking on future orders
options.B: Give the full ten, because a regular fitter is worth more than one order's margin
options.C: Offer what is inside your authority and ask for something of equal value in return, such as a bigger order
options.D: Promise the full ten now and sort out the approval with your manager afterwards

questions.stem: A regular asks for a volume rate above your authority and needs the parts before Monday. Which line is an honest Consequence step in the Commitment Close?

options.A: "This is the very last box we will have in stock, so if you don't take it now, it will be gone."
options.B: "You will regret it later if you don't order today, because most of our regulars already have."
options.C: "If we wait for the next level, you may not have the parts before Monday. If we move today at the current price, you're covered for this job."
options.D: "This price only holds until the end of today, so you really need to decide in the next hour or so."

questions.stem: A big trade account wants a rate you cannot approve. What does the course say keeps the customer loyal?

options.A: Say clearly what you cannot do and what you can, then follow up yourself on the day you said
options.B: Promise the rate today and hope that your manager agrees to it when you ask later
options.C: Pass the request to the next level and let the customer chase them directly for an answer on the rate
options.D: Give a soft "maybe" so the customer does not hear a no and stays in a good mood

questions.stem: Why does the course recommend giving a busy trade customer one or two clear options, rather than many?

options.A: Customers trust a counter more when it only stocks two versions of each part
options.B: Two options make it easier to steer the customer away from the cheaper choice toward the one you prefer
options.C: Too many choices stall people; one or two options in the customer's own terms help them decide
options.D: A short list means you never need to ask the customer what the job is for

questions.stem: A slow quarter hits the counter. According to the course, what is most likely to keep you employed through it?

options.A: Offering more extras to every customer, whatever the job actually needs
options.B: Reliability, honesty and consistency across the quiet hours
options.C: Promising quick delivery dates to win orders, then working out the details
options.D: Pushing harder on each customer to lift the numbers while trade is thin

questions.stem: Which three parts does the course say a strong review file contains?

options.A: Your numbers, your behavior entries, and what you improved along with an honest gap
options.B: A summary written the week before the review, focused on why you deserve more
options.C: Names and details of difficult customers, the dates they came in, and what they said
options.D: Your best sales, compliments from customers, and a list of what your coworkers did wrong

questions.stem: You are preparing to ask for a senior counter role using the Commitment Close. Where should the criteria come from?

options.A: From what a colleague thinks the role needs
options.B: From your manager, in their own words
options.C: From your own view of what you do best
options.D: From comparing yourself with the hardest worker

questions.stem: You make your case for a senior counter role and your manager says, "Not yet." What does the course say you should leave the conversation with?

options.A: A clear yes or no on whether you will ever be considered
options.B: A promise that you will get the next role that opens
options.C: Nothing more, since a "not yet" closes the subject
options.D: Concrete conditions and a date to review them

questions.stem: In what order do the five steps of the Commitment Close run?

options.A: Evidence, Criteria, Open question, Consequence, Genuine choice.
options.B: Criteria, Consequence, Evidence, Genuine choice, Open question.
options.C: Open question, Criteria, Evidence, Genuine choice, Consequence.
options.D: Criteria, Evidence, Consequence, Open question, Genuine choice.

questions.stem: In A.R.T., what does the Reframe step do?

options.A: Repeats the product's main features, so that the client can see why the price is fair for what they get.
options.B: Shifts the decision criterion from the visible cost to the cost of inaction, without defending features.
options.C: Offers a small concession on the price, so that the client feels the concern has been taken seriously.
options.D: Asks the client a yes or no question, so that the concern is closed before the call moves on.

questions.stem: According to the course, what separates strong output from survival?

options.A: It is faster: the rep makes more dials in each hour than anyone else on the team does.
options.B: It is tougher: the rep keeps every client on the line until they agree to a next step.
options.C: It is deliberate: the rep knows the goal and their own numbers before the session.
options.D: It is busier: the rep ends each session tired, which shows how much work was done.

questions.stem: Which of these is a goal in the sense the course means?

options.A: "Book one more next step per ten conversations by asking a clear how question at the end."
options.B: "Get better at calls this month."
options.C: "Have a much stronger month than the last one."
options.D: "Sound more confident with every client."

questions.stem: Which layer of numbers tells you where the process leaks?

options.A: Output numbers.
options.B: Conversion numbers.
options.C: Outcome numbers.
options.D: Revenue numbers for the quarter.

questions.stem: When you read the gap in your weekly numbers, what do you check first?

options.A: Whether output is steady.
options.B: Which client was hardest to deal with last week.
options.C: Whether the sales total beat the week before.
options.D: How your numbers compare with a colleague's.

questions.stem: Your lead asks for your weekly summary. Which version follows the course?

options.A: "I had a slow week because the leads were bad, but I'll smash it next week."
options.B: "My numbers were down, so next week I promise to double my meetings."
options.C: "Calls were steady, so activity was fine. My largest drop is between conversations and meetings. What would help you see the booking step most clearly, so that I can test one change there next week?"
options.D: "It was a tough week for everyone. Can you get us some better leads?"

questions.stem: What does the course say is your first job with your numbers?

options.A: Invent your own scoreboard, since most employers define their numbers poorly in writing.
options.B: Aim for the standard industry conversion rate that applies to every tele sales team.
options.C: Focus on the sales figure alone, since it is the number your employer is paid for.
options.D: Find the scoreboard your employer already uses and learn its definitions.

questions.stem: What is the one job of an opening?

options.A: To present the offer quickly, before the client has the chance to end the call or ask who is calling.
options.B: To impress the client with the organization's record, so that they take the rest of the call seriously.
options.C: To earn the next thirty seconds by giving the client a reason to stay and an easy way to say no.
options.D: To get the client to agree that now is a good time to talk, so that the pitch can start straight away.

questions.stem: Which cold-call opening follows the First-Contact Standard?

options.A: "Hi, this is the sales team calling. Do you have a second? It'll just take thirty seconds."
options.B: "Hello, we have a great offer on right now, and I think you'll want to hear about it today."
options.C: "Hi, is now a good time? I'd like to tell you about our service before the offer ends."
options.D: "Good morning, this is (your name) from (your organization). If this is not a good moment, say so and I will close the file for today. I am calling because firms like yours have been asking us about payments reporting. How does your team handle that reporting at the moment?"

questions.stem: A gatekeeper gives you a firm no. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Write the decline down and try another route or another day.
options.B: Ask again more firmly, since gatekeepers are trained to refuse the first request.
options.C: Say you are returning the decision-maker's call, so that you are put through.
options.D: Keep the gatekeeper talking until they agree to pass on a short message.

questions.stem: You are returning a call the client asked for. Which question fits the Curiosity step?

options.A: "Are you ready to go ahead with the order today?"
options.B: "What has changed since we last spoke?"
options.C: "Why did you want me to call you back this week?"
options.D: "Can I take you through our full list of features first?"

questions.stem: Which call note follows the course?

options.A: "14 March, 10:40. Client said the current supplier 'missed two of the last four delivery windows.' Agreed I call back Thursday 21 March at 11:00 with a delivery schedule for their region."
options.B: "Called. Interested, will think about it. Follow up soon."
options.C: "Logistics issue with current supplier. Good prospect. Send info."
options.D: "Spoke to buyer, friendly call. Card details taken for later."

questions.stem: What must every open contact in your pipeline carry?

options.A: A note that the client is interested, with a reminder to follow up at some point next week.
options.B: A next step with a day and a time, said out loud and written down.
options.C: A discount offer that is ready to use if the client goes quiet after the first conversation.
options.D: A copy of the client's full payment and address details, so that the order can move fast.

questions.stem: A contact has gone quiet after two attempts. What is the honest move?

options.A: Keep the contact open in the pipeline, so that the total opportunity looks healthy.
options.B: Call every day until the client answers, so that they know you are still interested.
options.C: Send a message saying the offer ends this week, so that the client has a reason to reply.
options.D: Send one clear, low-pressure message, then close the log entry unless they reply.

questions.stem: A client asks not to be called again. When do you log the request?

options.A: At the end of the shift, with the rest of the day's notes.
options.B: After one more call to check that the client really means it.
options.C: At once, before you do anything else.
options.D: When your lead next reviews the call list with you.

questions.stem: A client raises their voice. What does the course say most reps do wrong, and what should you do instead?
