options.A: Most reps go quiet; talk more, so that the client can hear you are in control.
options.B: Most reps listen too long; move straight to explaining what went wrong.
options.C: Most reps stay calm; match the client's energy, so that they feel taken seriously.
options.D: Most reps speed up; slow down by about a notch.

questions.stem: On a hot call, when do you use the Mandatory Pause?

options.A: Before you answer the call, and again before you end it.
options.B: Only when the client asks you to stop talking for a moment.
options.C: After the client finishes, and after you name their feeling.
options.D: After you explain the process, and again after you apologize.

questions.stem: A client says, "This is my third call and still no answer." Which acknowledgment is accurate and safe?

options.A: "You're right, we've been useless on this one."
options.B: "That sounds exhausting, three calls and no answer."
options.C: "I understand, but here is how our process works."
options.D: "I can hear you're upset, so let me explain what happened."

questions.stem: A client demands a manager. What should you do?

options.A: Accept the request and ask what they need the manager to be able to do for them today.
options.B: Say the manager is not available and that there is nothing more you can do on this call.
options.C: Promise that the manager will call back within the hour with a delivery date for the order.
options.D: Ask the client why they want a manager when you are able to deal with the matter yourself.

questions.stem: You list three gaps that keep repeating in your calls. Which one do you choose to work on?

options.A: The one that appears most often.
options.B: The one that feels most embarrassing.
options.C: The one that is easiest to hide from your lead.
options.D: All three together, to save time.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a gap you can actually fix?

options.A: "I'm bad at handling objections."
options.B: "I'm just not a natural on the phone."
options.C: "The clients in my list are simply much harder to sell to than everyone else's."
options.D: "I lose the call when a client says the current supplier is fine."

questions.stem: What does a test of a fix consist of?

options.A: Three changes, one measure, one month.
options.B: One change, no measure, until it feels right.
options.C: One change, one measure, one week.
options.D: Two changes, two measures, one week.

questions.stem: After a week, your number has risen, but the change works by crowding the client into a next step. What does the course say?

options.A: Keep it, because the number is the only thing that the test was set up to measure.
options.B: It is not a fix; keep only changes that are both effective and honest.
options.C: Keep it for a month and review it only if a client makes a formal complaint about it.
options.D: Add a second change next week, so that the crowding is less obvious to the client.

questions.stem: A client asks for a price below what you are allowed to give. Which reply follows the course?

options.A: "I totally understand. Let me see what I can do on the price for you."
options.B: "It sounds like the number needs to work harder for you. What would this delay cost you over the next quarter? If the price stays as it is, what would need to be true for it to make sense?"
options.C: "I'm sure we can sort something out. Shall I send a revised quote?"
options.D: "I hear you, but our price is fair when you look at all the features."

questions.stem: You have authority to waive a set-up fee. How does the course say a concession like this should be used?

options.A: Given straight away, to end an uncomfortable moment on the call.
options.B: Hinted at early, so that the client stays interested in the offer.
options.C: Traded for something of equal value, such as a longer commitment.
options.D: Kept back and never mentioned, whatever the client proposes.

questions.stem: A client says, "Stop calling me." What do you do?

options.A: Confirm it, log it at once, and offer no check-back.
options.B: Ask whether you could check back in six months, then log their answer.
options.C: Ask one more question about their supplier before you end the call.
options.D: Note it at the end of the week, when you tidy up your whole call list.

questions.stem: A client asks you to confirm a saving you cannot back with evidence. Which reply follows the course?

options.A: "Most clients in your sector save about that much, so you can count on it."
options.B: "I can't promise it, but between us, you will almost certainly see that saving."
options.C: "Everyone is switching to us this year, so the saving more or less speaks for itself."
options.D: "I don't want to give you a number I can't stand behind. What I can confirm today is the part I know. What would be most useful for me to send you in writing?"

questions.stem: Which question should you bring to a quality review?

options.A: "Why did I get such a low score on this call?"
options.B: "Can you raise the score if I explain what I meant?"
options.C: "What would a stronger first three minutes look like on this call?"
options.D: "Is this the same checklist that everyone else on the team is scored against?"

questions.stem: A reviewer flags one weak moment on one call in an otherwise strong month. How do you read it fairly?

options.A: As noise from a single call; the same weak moment across three calls would be a signal.
options.B: As proof that you are bad at the job and that your strong month was down to luck.
options.C: As an unfair comment, since a colleague does the same thing and was not flagged for it.
options.D: As something to ignore completely, since single flags never point to anything real.

questions.stem: What should you ask the retention team for?

options.A: The names and contact details of the clients who cancelled, so that you can call them back.
options.B: Everything they hold on your last fifty clients, so that you can look through it for ideas.
options.C: Their opinion on which reps in the team are causing the most cancellations this quarter.
options.D: The pattern, never the person: what clients most often say when they cancel.

questions.stem: What should a quality review leave you with?

options.A: A list of five improvements to work on at the same time before the next review comes round.
options.B: One change, small enough to try next session and specific enough to hear yourself doing it.
options.C: A general aim to ask better questions and to sound more confident on every call you make.
options.D: A higher score, agreed with the reviewer after you have explained what you meant on the call.

questions.stem: Before every one-to-one, the course asks for a three-line weekly brief. What are the three lines?

options.A: Your best call of the week, the client who was hardest to deal with, and the reason your targets should be lowered.
options.B: The hours you worked, the number of dials you made, and a request for better leads for the coming week.
options.C: Your forecast for the month, your colleagues' numbers for comparison, and a list of problems for your lead to solve.
options.D: Where your numbers stand against target, the one thing you are changing this week, and what you need from your lead, as a question.

questions.stem: How should you defend a forecast to your lead?

options.A: State the number, the deals behind it, what must be true for each, and the one that worries you.
options.B: Round the number up a little, so that your lead can see how confident you are about the month ahead.
options.C: Give the number only, and explain the detail later if your lead asks you a question about it.
options.D: Leave out any deal that worries you, so that the forecast looks solid when your lead reads it.

questions.stem: You want to be considered for larger accounts. Which ask follows the course?

options.A: "I've worked hard this year and I think I deserve a shot at the bigger accounts. Can I have them?"
options.B: "I'd like to take on two of the larger dormant accounts and run them for six weeks with a weekly check-in. What would you need to see from me to make that a fair test?"
options.C: "Give me the bigger accounts and I promise I will close every one of them this quarter."
options.D: "I'm not sure my targets are realistic with these leads. Could the bigger accounts fix that?"

questions.stem: When you ask for a stretch account, what may you promise your lead?

options.A: That the account will close before the test period ends.
options.B: That the account will definitely pay off for the team.
options.C: The work, the reporting and the check-in, not the outcome.
options.D: That you will hit every one of your targets while you are running it.

questions.stem: What does the course mean by consistency?

options.A: Your worst week is still acceptable.
options.B: Your best week is far above the target.
options.C: Your weeks average out across the month.
options.D: Your numbers are the same as your colleagues'.

questions.stem: Mid-call, a client asks for something and you are not sure it is allowed under the rules. What do you do?

options.A: Agree to it now and check with your lead after the sale has gone through.
options.B: Make your best guess, since stopping to check would lose the client's interest.
options.C: Say you will check and come back, and then do it.
options.D: Refuse it at once and tell the client that the rules never allow exceptions.

questions.stem: Which four kinds of evidence build a promotion case?

options.A: Length of service, the hours you have worked, praise from clients, and a statement that you feel ready for the next step now.
options.B: Monthly numbers against target, specific wins with the story attached, evidence of how you work with others, and the role you want with the gap named.
options.C: Your best month, your biggest sale, your manager's opinion of you, and a request to be considered for the next opening.
options.D: Your dial count, your talk time, your attendance record, and a promise to hit a higher number once you are promoted.

questions.stem: Which line belongs in the running file behind a promotion case?

options.A: "Was great on the phone all week."
options.B: "Felt much more confident with clients."
options.C: "Deserve the senior role more than anyone."
options.D: "Handled a client escalation and handed it over cleanly."

questions.stem: Which list gives the five steps of the Commitment Close in the order this course teaches?

options.A: Criteria, Consequence, Evidence, Genuine choice, Calibrated question
options.B: Evidence, Criteria, Genuine choice, Consequence, Calibrated question
options.C: Criteria, Evidence, Consequence, Calibrated question, Genuine choice
options.D: Consequence, Criteria, Evidence, Calibrated question, Genuine choice

questions.stem: A seller makes a first call to an operations lead who did not expect it. Which opening follows the First-Contact Standard?

options.A: "This is (your name) from (your company). We help businesses like yours cut costs with our platform. Do you have five minutes to hear how it works?"
options.B: "This is (your name) from (your company). Before we go further, what is your budget for this year, and who signs off on new suppliers?"
options.C: "This is (your name) from (your company). Our platform is the best on the market and this offer ends Friday, so can I book you a demo now?"
options.D: "This is (your name) from (your company). Tell me if now is wrong and I'll call back. Teams your size say late delivery notices cost them repeat orders. Is that close to your situation?"

questions.stem: Earlier in the call, a client said slow handovers cost the team hours each week. Now the client says, "This costs more than we budgeted." Which reply follows A.R.T.?

options.A: "The price is what it is, and it reflects the quality you get. Shall I send the proposal over anyway so you can review it?"
options.B: "I understand, but our platform does much more than what you use now. Let me send you a full feature comparison so you can see the difference."
options.C: "That's fair. Let me check with my manager whether we can bring the figure down to match what you budgeted for this year."
options.D: "It sounds like the figure landed above what you planned for. The way I'd look at it is what the slow handovers cost your team each month. What would you need to see to compare the two?"

questions.stem: A seller reviews three real deals from the first months and sees the same weak habit in all three. What does the course recommend doing with this baseline?

options.A: Name that one habit clearly and pick the specific situation where the replacement will be practiced this week
options.B: Write a list of ten things to improve and work on all of them at once
options.C: Treat the result as a verdict on whether they are suited to the role at all
options.D: Keep the baseline private and act on it at the next quarterly review

questions.stem: Your employer sets a quarterly revenue target that feels heavy and vague. What does the course suggest you do first to make it workable?

options.A: Ask your manager to lower the target before you start, since nobody can plan against a number that feels this heavy and vague
options.B: Wait until the middle of the quarter and then judge whether it was realistic
options.C: Break it into a chain of figures (conversations, proposals, closes, deal size) to find a weekly number you control
options.D: Ignore the revenue figure and focus only on how many calls you make

questions.stem: The course uses a "control test": can you do it today, regardless of what any client decides? Which measure passes that test as an activity (lead) measure?

options.A: Margin achieved on last month's deals
options.B: The number of proposals you send this week
options.C: Revenue closed this quarter across all of your accounts
options.D: Accounts retained over the year

questions.stem: Your pipeline report shows six open opportunities. Three of them have no next step at all. How does the course describe those three?

options.A: As your safest deals, since nothing has gone wrong with them yet and no client has said no
options.B: As proof that the report is broken and should be ignored for now
options.C: As hopes, not forecast; each needs a dated next step or an honest decision
options.D: As deals to delete quietly so that the forecast looks cleaner

questions.stem: In a one-to-one about how your measures are built, your manager says something that sounds like a promise about your bonus. What does the course tell you to do?

options.A: Write nothing down, so the conversation stays informal and friendly
options.B: Act on it straight away, since your own manager said it
options.C: Ask for it in writing through the normal channel before acting on it
options.D: Tell your colleagues about it so that they can ask the manager for the same arrangement

questions.stem: A seller keeps delaying new accounts because they want to research each one fully first. What standard does the course set for adding an account to the list?

options.A: It belongs on the list once you can name one true reason to reach out
options.B: It belongs on the list once you have built a full profile of the business
options.C: It belongs on the list once a colleague confirms they know the company
options.D: It belongs on the list once your manager has approved it in a review

questions.stem: Where does the course suggest looking first to find a reason to reach out, without spending an hour on each account?

options.A: A general list of the largest employers in the region you cover
options.B: The account's size, since bigger accounts always have the bigger needs
options.C: A change in the business, such as a new site, a hiring push or an expansion
options.D: Your own newest product, since it always gives you something fresh and interesting to introduce

questions.stem: In your weekly clean-out you find a dormant account. You contacted it months ago, got no engagement, and cannot write one true reason to reach out now. What does the course's rule say?

options.A: Call it this week anyway with a general introduction, since any contact is better than none
options.B: Take it off the active list; it can come back later with a new reason
options.C: Keep it on the active list in case something comes up later on
options.D: Mark it closed permanently and never consider the account again

questions.stem: You think an account may have a supplier problem, but you are not sure. How should you write your reason to reach out?

options.A: Leave the reason out and open with a short introduction of your offer
options.B: State the problem as a fact, because a confident reason earns more attention
options.C: Add a short deadline so the client feels they need to answer you quickly
options.D: Say so honestly, for example "I don't know whether this is an issue for you"

questions.stem: On a cold call, a buyer says "Just send me an email." You make one calm pivot, and the buyer repeats "Just email me." What do you do next?

options.A: Pivot a second time with a stronger reason, since a reflex brush-off can usually be turned around
options.B: Treat it as a genuine decline, end the call respectfully and log it
options.C: Keep talking until the buyer agrees to at least a short meeting
options.D: Offer a discount so the buyer stays on the line a little longer

questions.stem: A colleague has introduced you to a buyer. Which approach uses the warm introduction the way the course teaches?

options.A: Say who you are and who sent you, offer to come back if this is a bad week, give the one reason they were suggested, and ask one open question
options.B: Skip the introduction and pitch your offer at once, since your colleague has already done the work for you
options.C: Tell the buyer your colleague strongly advised them to decide this week, so the timing works for everyone
options.D: Tell the buyer your colleague said they need your service, then ask straight away when the two of you can meet

questions.stem: You want to open a cold call by saying the buyer's sites closed for repairs last month, but you cannot verify it. What does the course say?

options.A: Use it, but say it quickly so it sounds less like a claim and more like a fact
options.B: Do not use it; open with a reason you can verify, such as a published expansion
options.C: Use it anyway, since most buyers will not stop to check a detail like that during a short cold call
options.D: Replace it with a claim about how much downtime your own product can cut

questions.stem: You have a three-day week and twenty accounts to contact. What is the honest approach?

options.A: Contact the few with the strongest checkable reason well, and give the rest a dated note
options.B: Drop outreach completely this week and catch up on it next week
options.C: Add a short deadline to every message to force a quicker reply
options.D: Contact all twenty quickly, with a short opener that skips the reason, so no account is left out this week

questions.stem: Across three calls, a client has given you only facts: site counts, volumes and equipment age. The deal is not moving. What does the course tell you to do?

options.A: Keep collecting situation facts until the client volunteers a problem on their own
options.B: Ask sharper, faster questions to show the client you are serious about the deal and short on time
options.C: Add urgency so the client feels they must open up before the quarter ends
options.D: Lower the cost of answering honestly and climb the question ladder one rung at a time

questions.stem: A client has mentioned late deliveries in every call so far. Which question best tests the impact of this repeating gap?

options.A: "You've mentioned late deliveries three times now. What happens on a week when a delivery runs two days late?"
options.B: "Our system would solve your late deliveries. Shall we go ahead and set up a trial next week?"
options.C: "How many deliveries does your team make each week, and how many vehicles do you run?"
options.D: "Why do you keep having late deliveries when you already have two warehouse sites running?"

questions.stem: A deal has stalled because a finance figure sits with someone you cannot reach. You take it to your manager. What should you bring?

options.A: A request for permission to offer the client a discount, since a lower price usually moves a stalled deal
options.B: A forwarded email chain and a request that your manager sorts it out
options.C: The situation in one line, what you have already tried, and a specific recommendation
options.D: A list of complaints about how slow the client's finance team has been

questions.stem: Which rung of the question ladder does the course call the one most sellers skip, and the one that builds the case for change?

options.A: Need
options.B: Impact
options.C: Situation
options.D: Problem

questions.stem: A client sharply says your fee is unreasonable and asks whether you are serious. What should you do first?

options.A: Explain the pricing again in more detail and compare it with what competitors charge for similar work
options.B: Offer a small discount straight away to end the discomfort on both sides
options.C: Answer the client's tone with a firm defense of your quality and service
options.D: Hold the Mandatory Pause for a few seconds, then label the client's feeling

questions.stem: Which Acknowledge line fits A.R.T. as this course teaches it?

options.A: "I can hear you're frustrated. Shall we look at a smaller package?"
options.B: "It sounds like the number landed harder than you expected."
options.C: "I can see the number is a shock, but it reflects our quality."
options.D: "I understand how you feel, but many clients pay this amount."

questions.stem: A client told you the current process loses about a week of work each quarter. Now the client says the implementation fee is far too high. Which Reframe fits A.R.T.?

options.A: "Our implementation is the most complete one available, so the fee simply reflects that level of work."
options.B: "If the fee is the main problem, I can check with my manager whether a lower rate is possible."
options.C: "You mentioned the current process loses a week of work each quarter. If that continues for a year, the costs add up; the fee is paid once."
options.D: "Other clients your size pay exactly the same fee, and none of them has raised it as a concern."

questions.stem: A client's concern moves from budget to timing to team workload and back to budget. Which question does the course suggest to find the hidden driver?

options.A: "What happened the last time you signed an agreement like this?"
options.B: "Can we settle the budget question first, before anything else?"
options.C: "Why do your concerns keep changing every time we speak?"
options.D: "What would you do if we were able to lower the price for you?"

questions.stem: In a buying group, which role describes someone who can stop or slow the deal, often because the change costs them budget, control or workload?

options.A: Influencer
options.B: Blocker
options.C: Decider
options.D: Champion

questions.stem: You learn that a finance controller and an IT lead are involved in a deal you have worked only through your contact. What is the honest way to reach them?

options.A: Wait until the two of them contact you, so you do not upset anyone inside
options.B: Ask your contact to forward your proposal to the two of them and hope it reaches the right people in time
options.C: Ask your contact how they would like to be involved, then reach the others with their knowledge
options.D: Contact the two of them directly without telling your contact, to save time

questions.stem: You prepare messages for three stakeholders in the same deal: operations, finance and IT. What keeps this honest?

options.A: Each message lists every feature in full, so that no one can say they missed something
options.B: Only the decider gets a message, since the others cannot sign the agreement anyway
options.C: Each person gets a different promise that fits what they most want to hear, so that every stakeholder feels looked after
options.D: Each message uses the same offer and facts, and leads with the part that answers that person's interest

questions.stem: Late in a deal, a procurement contact says, "Your figure is high; we have a lower offer." Which response fits A.R.T.?

options.A: "The other supplier cuts corners, so their number is not really comparable with ours. Our clients stay with us because we deliver what we promise."
options.B: "You want to be sure the cost is right for what you get. The question is what the lower number includes over the term. What would help you compare the two on total cost?"
options.C: "I understand, but our quality is far higher than theirs. If it helps, I can ask whether we can match their figure this time."
options.D: "Why do you think our price is high? Most of our clients see it as fair once they understand everything that comes with it."

questions.stem: Which request to a busy schedules team fits the course?

options.A: "Please put my account at the top of your list this week. My quota depends on it, and my manager is watching."
options.B: "I need the confirmed delivery date for this account before I meet their operations lead on Thursday. If I have it by Wednesday, I can lock their start. What would you need from me to confirm it by then?"
options.C: "Could you send me every delivery date you have planned for this quarter, so I can work out which ones apply to my accounts?"
options.D: "Hi, could you check the delivery slot for this account when you get a chance? No rush, whenever suits you. Thanks."

questions.stem: You need a finance colleague to look at a client's situation. What does the course say about client details in that written request?

options.A: Make the request by phone only, so that there is no written record of it at all
options.B: Paste the whole client file into the email so the colleague has everything they need and does not have to ask
options.C: Send the details through a personal messaging app so that the request moves faster
options.D: Do not copy personal data from the client file into the email; describe the situation instead

questions.stem: You are preparing for a forecast call. Which of these counts as evidence for a deal?

options.A: The client proposed a meeting date and sent their requirements document
options.B: You have a strong feeling, based on your experience, that this particular deal is going to close
options.C: The contact sounded positive and friendly throughout the last call
options.D: The deal has been sitting in your pipeline for a long time already

questions.stem: According to the course, a good note on a live deal answers which three things?

options.A: How the client felt, what you think of them, and your chance of winning
options.B: Who called whom, how long the call lasted, and the time it took place
options.C: What the client said, what you promised, and what happens next
options.D: Your price, your discount limit, and the price your competitor quoted

questions.stem: Which ending gives a real next step as the course defines it?

options.A: "Shall we set up another call sometime soon to go over the proposal together in more detail?"
options.B: "I'll send over some more information on the pilot after this call, and you can take a look."
options.C: "What would work better: a short call with your operations lead on Thursday, or a written summary she can read on Friday?"
options.D: "Thanks for your time today. We'll be in touch soon about the next stage of this."

questions.stem: In the Commitment Close, what does the Consequence step ask you to do?

options.A: Remind the client how much time you have already invested in the deal
options.B: Warn the client that the price will rise if they do not sign this week, so they see the cost of delay
options.C: List every feature the client will miss out on without your offer
options.D: Name the consequences honestly, including when waiting is better for the client

questions.stem: The client's budget does not open until April, and waiting is genuinely the right call. What does the course tell you to do?

options.A: Say waiting makes sense, then agree a date, a person and something that will be true by then
options.B: Invent a price change so that the client brings the decision forward
options.C: Stop contacting the client until April and wait for them to call you when the budget is ready
options.D: Push for a signature now, before the client's attention moves elsewhere

questions.stem: A client asks you to confirm a start date that depends on another team. What should you say?

options.A: That you cannot confirm it yourself, when you will have an answer, and what to plan around
options.B: Confirm the date now to keep the deal moving, and sort out the details with the other team later
options.C: Tell the client the date will probably hold, since the other team usually manages to deliver on time
options.D: Leave the date out of the conversation for now and only come back to it if the client raises it again

questions.stem: Which three things does the course say most employers reward in a selling role?

options.A: Effort, enthusiasm in team meetings, and the largest contact list on the team
options.B: Time in the role, a close friendship with the manager, and a confident manner
options.C: Long working hours, being liked by colleagues, and one very strong month of sales that everyone remembers
options.D: Documented results, predictability, and behavior that makes you easy to trust with bigger accounts

questions.stem: How does the course suggest keeping your record?

options.A: Notes written once at the end of each year, focused on the biggest wins you remember
options.B: One page with the date, the deal or task, what you did and the documented outcome, added to every week
options.C: A file holding every client's personal details, so that nothing important is ever lost
options.D: A list of your best moments only, written up from memory whenever a performance review is getting close to the date

questions.stem: You are building a case for promotion. On one of your manager's three criteria, your evidence is thin. What does the course recommend?

options.A: Ask your manager to drop that criterion just for your case
options.B: Leave that criterion out so the case looks as strong as possible
options.C: Promise your manager you will be strong there once promoted
options.D: Name the thin spot openly and propose a specific way to test it

questions.stem: Your month is heading below target with three weeks left. What does the course say is the strongest move?

options.A: Speak to your manager early, with a diagnosis, a recommendation and a how or what question
options.B: Explain the reasons at length and apologize until your manager stops asking
options.C: Tell clients that availability is limited this month to speed up their decisions
options.D: Stay quiet, keep working, and hope that next month makes up for the gap

questions.stem: Which list gives the five steps of the Commitment Close in the correct order?

options.A: Criteria, Consequence, Evidence, Genuine choice, Calibrated question
options.B: Criteria, Evidence, Consequence, Calibrated question, Genuine choice
options.C: Anchor, Evidence, Consequence, Calibrated question, Genuine choice
options.D: Situation, Problem, Impact, Need, Genuine choice

questions.stem: A customer has told you that their internet connection drops every evening. You want to move to the Impact rung of the Question Ladder. Which question do you ask?

options.A: "What is happening with your connection at the moment, day to day?"
options.B: "What would a good outcome look like for you?"
options.C: "Why did you wait until now to report this?"
options.D: "What does losing the connection each evening cost you?"

questions.stem: Your first probation checkpoint is next week. Which day-to-day signals does a team lead notice and remember at checkpoint time?

options.A: Clear case notes, follow-through on what you said, and your tone under pressure
options.B: How often you remind the team lead that you want to pass probation and take on more
options.C: How fast you close each contact, even when the customer has to come back later
options.D: How your dashboard numbers compare with a friend's numbers at another employer

questions.stem: In your first measured week you feel watched. You rush the end of contacts, forget to log a case and skip a follow-up. What explains this, and what protects you from it?

options.A: It is a character flaw, and the fix is to try harder and push through on every contact
options.B: You have forgotten the frameworks, so the fix is to reread all four before every shift
options.C: Anxiety narrows attention; automatic habits like the three-part message and case note survive it
options.D: Mistakes are expected while you are being measured, so nothing in your daily routine needs to change

questions.stem: A customer is delighted with your help and rates the contact highly. The reviewer finds that you skipped a required verification step. Which number drops, and for what reason?

options.A: Quality score, because it is built from the employer's checklist, not the customer's feeling
options.B: Customer satisfaction, because the reviewer's finding overrides the rating the customer gave
options.C: Handle time, because the reviewer adds the skipped step's time back onto the contact
options.D: First-contact resolution, because any skipped step is counted as a repeat contact on your record

questions.stem: Your handle time is over target. Which change is an honest way to improve it?

options.A: Transfer long contacts to a colleague so that your clock starts again
options.B: End the contact as soon as you have given the main answer, even if the customer is still asking
options.C: Prepare what you might need before the contact, and say one clear sentence instead of three
options.D: Ask the customer to contact you again later about the second part of the problem

questions.stem: You are about to end a contact and want to protect first-contact resolution. Which closing check do you use?

options.A: "Is everything clear now?"
options.B: "Is there anything else I can help you with?"
options.C: "Would you be happy to rate this contact well in the survey?"
options.D: "What will you do first if this happens again?"

questions.stem: Your team lead says, "Your handle time is over target this month." Which response fits the course?

options.A: "I know, but my cases are harder than everyone else's, so the average is misleading this month."
options.B: "Thank you for showing me. Which should we look at first: my longest contacts, or the ones that came back?"
options.C: "Understood. From tomorrow I will end every single contact faster until the number is back under the target."
options.D: "Handle time is unfair to people who take care with customers, so I focus on the other numbers."

questions.stem: A busy hour is starting and several contacts are waiting. What do you do before you take the next one?

options.A: Scan the queue for a few seconds: how long each has waited, which are urgent, which are repeats
options.B: Take the contacts strictly in the order they appear, so every customer is treated the same way
options.C: Clear all the quickest contacts first so the queue looks shorter, then go back to the hard ones
options.D: Take the newest contact first while it is fresh, because the older ones have waited anyway

questions.stem: You told the customer in chat A, "I'll be back in two minutes." Chat B now needs you urgently and you cannot return to A in time. What do you do about chat A?

options.A: Stay silent until you are free, because the final answer matters more than the wait
options.B: Close chat A and ask the customer to start a new chat later
options.C: Send a quick line such as "Still here, one more check" so the promise is updated
options.D: Send chat A your best guess at the answer so that the loop is closed

questions.stem: A caller's issue belongs to the billing team and cannot wait. What do you do before you transfer the call?

options.A: Transfer straight away, because explaining first only adds to your handle time and theirs
options.B: Tell the customer what is happening, what you passed on, and what happens when they get there
options.C: Put the customer on hold without a reason, then transfer the call when billing finally picks up
options.D: Give the customer the billing team's direct number and ask them to call it themselves now

questions.stem: A customer emails, upset that the same problem has happened twice. Your template opens with "Thank you for contacting us." How do you make the reply personal without adding real time?

options.A: Send the template exactly as written, because templates protect your speed and keep replies consistent
options.B: Add more formal wording and a long apology at the top, so the customer sees the company takes it seriously
options.C: Remove the greeting and paste the full knowledge base article underneath, so every detail is covered
options.D: Match the opening to what they said, use one detail from their message, and close with a real choice

questions.stem: A customer asks for a full refund after the refund window has closed. A partial refund is still possible. In which order do you speak?

options.A: The options first, so that the no sounds softer when it comes
options.B: The limit first, once and with a plain reason, then the options that truly exist
options.C: The policy several times, more firmly each time, until the customer accepts it
options.D: An exception first, which you will check with your team lead after the contact

questions.stem: After your refusal the customer says, "I've been a customer for five years, and this is how you treat me?" Which line is a correct Acknowledge step of A.R.T.?

options.A: "It sounds like you are upset, but the refund window is closed."
options.B: "I can see why you think that, though the policy is the same for everyone."
options.C: "Why do you feel that we are treating you badly?"
options.D: "It sounds like after five years this feels personal."

questions.stem: You want to follow a no with two options. One of them you have confirmed. The other you think is probably available, but you have not checked. What do you do?

options.A: Offer both now, because two options sound more generous than one and the customer will feel valued
options.B: Offer both, and quietly withdraw the second one later on if it turns out not to be available to them after all
options.C: Offer only the confirmed option, because a choice is real only if every option is true and yours to offer
options.D: Offer no options at all, and repeat the limit calmly until the customer accepts it and moves on

questions.stem: A customer pushes back on a refusal. The representative repeats the policy, more firmly each time, and the customer pushes harder each time. What explains this?

options.A: Repeating the policy adds pressure, and pressure creates resistance: the refusal feels like a corner
options.B: The customer did not hear the policy clearly, so it needs to be said once more in plainer words
options.C: The customer has already decided to get a manager, and nothing a representative says can change that
options.D: The representative has not yet explained enough of the history and the reasons behind the policy

questions.stem: A customer contacts you for the third time about the same unresolved problem. How does the course tell you to use the Question Ladder here?

options.A: Give the customer the full timeline of what happened on the first two contacts
options.B: Ask an Impact question such as "How is this affecting your day right now?"
options.C: Treat it as a fresh start and ask the customer to explain it all from the beginning
options.D: Ask, "Why do you keep contacting us about this?"

questions.stem: A caller starts swearing at you. Your employer's policy says you may warn once and then end the contact. What do you say?

options.A: "It sounds like this has made you really angry. I want to sort it out. I can't keep going while I'm being sworn at."
options.B: "Please calm down. I cannot help you with anything until you calm down and stop shouting at me."
options.C: "I understand that you are angry, but shouting at me will not change the policy or the outcome here."
options.D: Nothing. You end the contact at once without a warning, because swearing is never acceptable.

questions.stem: A chat customer writes, "I want your manager. You are useless." What is your first move?

options.A: Explain what you have already done on the case, so the customer can see that you handled it correctly
options.B: Promise that a manager will call within the hour, to bring the temperature down
options.C: Ask, "Are you sure you need a manager for this?"
options.D: Name the loss of confidence, then ask, "What would you want the manager to be able to do for you here?"

questions.stem: A customer says, "I'll post this everywhere if you don't refund me today." The refund is outside policy. What drives your resolution?

options.A: The threat: approve the refund, because the company's public reputation matters more than the policy
options.B: A trade: offer something extra if the customer agrees not to post
options.C: The facts of the case and your employer's policy: offer no more and no less because of the threat
options.D: The tone: tell the customer that you cannot help anyone who makes threats

questions.stem: A delayed order now sits with the delivery team. Nothing about a release date is confirmed. Which message do you send the customer?

options.A: "I've escalated this to our delivery team, and they will look into it for you. Anything else I can help with?"
options.B: "Good news: it will be released tomorrow, so you can stop worrying and expect it in the next few days."
options.C: "We will be in touch as soon as we know more. Thank you for your patience while the team looks into it."
options.D: "Your order is at the depot. I've passed it to the delivery team. You'll hear from me Thursday by noon. Message or call?"

questions.stem: You checked that an order has left the warehouse. You did not check where it is now. What do you write on the "what is verified" line of your three-line case note?

options.A: "Order is on its way to the customer and should arrive in the next few days."
options.B: "Customer upset about the delay. Promised to sort it out as soon as possible."
options.C: "Order left the warehouse (checked). Current location not verified."
options.D: "Escalated to the delivery team. Customer awaiting an update."

questions.stem: The billing team has not answered about a refund, and your promised update to the customer is due tomorrow. How do you chase billing?

options.A: Send what the customer needs, what is already known and verified, and the date the customer was promised
options.B: Copy the billing manager into your chase and list everything the billing team has got wrong on this case so far
options.C: Do not chase again, because asking twice makes you look like you are nagging another team
options.D: Skip the chase and give the customer the date that you personally think is the most likely

questions.stem: A colleague goes on leave. One of their open cases shows that the customer was promised a call on Friday. The case is passed to you. What do you do?

options.A: Leave the case alone until your colleague returns, because the promise was theirs and not yours
options.B: Take it over, update the note, and make sure the Friday call happens, even if it only gives a new date
options.C: Message the customer that your colleague is away and ask them to get back in touch next week
options.D: Close the case, because the last note in the system does not show any open problem that needs action from you

questions.stem: A caller says, "Just cancel it. I don't want to discuss it." You suspect there is a fixable problem underneath. What do you say first?

options.A: "Thank you for being direct. The cancellation is yours to make. Before I set it up, what's changed?"
options.B: "Before you decide, let me remind you of all the benefits you would be giving up if you cancel today."
options.C: "Of course. Just so I can note it on the account, why do you want to cancel?"
options.D: "Are you sure about this? Most customers who cancel end up regretting it later."

questions.stem: A customer has decided to cancel. The representative keeps pressing on what the customer will lose by leaving. What effect does the course say this usually has?

options.A: The customer stays, because fear of losing something is the strongest reason to stay
options.B: Nothing changes, because the decision was already made before the contact started
options.C: Trust grows, because the customer sees the representative fighting hard to keep them
options.D: The customer defends the decision harder, and pressure becomes a new reason to leave

questions.stem: In a Commitment Close a representative says, "Staying on the current plan keeps all five seats at the full price. Moving to the smaller plan lowers the cost, and adding seats later would need a new request." Which step is this?

options.A: Criteria
options.B: Consequence
options.C: Evidence
options.D: Genuine choice

questions.stem: A customer has heard both real options and says, politely and firmly, "Neither. I'm done." What do you do?

options.A: Repeat both options once more, slowly and clearly, in case the customer missed something important in them
options.B: Ask, "Are you completely sure about this? Once it is done, it cannot be undone."
options.C: Process it cleanly, say what happens and when, and ask, "What email should the confirmation go to?"
options.D: Explain what the customer will lose by leaving, then offer the two options a second time

questions.stem: You are reading your scorecard for the second time and writing down each miss. Which note is written in behavioral words?

options.A: "Was careless and rushed at the end of the contact."
options.B: "Did not confirm the delivery date before ending the contact."
options.C: "Needs a much better attitude when closing contacts."
options.D: "Does not seem to care enough about getting the details right."

questions.stem: You review one of your own recordings in three passes. What do you look at in the second pass?

options.A: The facts: whether you verified the customer, stated the next step and got every detail right
options.B: Your questions: whether each question you asked started with how or what, or with why
options.C: Turn-taking: how often you spoke over the customer, and the gap before your first word
options.D: The customer: the moments where they caused the contact to go wrong, so you can note them

questions.stem: Your team lead says, "Your empathy statements sound scripted." You feel your jaw tighten. Which response fits the course?

options.A: "I hear you, but that customer was already angry before I said anything to them."
options.B: Say nothing in the meeting, then dispute the feedback in writing later, once you have had time to calm down
options.C: "So do you want me to stop using empathy statements altogether, then?"
options.D: Say back what you heard, then ask, "What would it have sounded like if it had landed as genuine?"

questions.stem: Which goal fits the one-page personal improvement plan?

options.A: "In my next ten contacts I'll name the feeling before explaining the process; I'll check on Friday."
options.B: "From now on I will be more empathetic with every customer I speak to, especially the difficult ones."
options.C: "This week I will fix my greeting, my pace, verification, empathy and my close."
options.D: "By the end of the month I will get a higher score than anyone else on my team."

questions.stem: By mid-afternoon, small things in a contact land harder on you than they did in the morning. How does the course explain this?

options.A: Customers become more difficult and less patient as the working day goes on
options.B: You are weaker under pressure than your colleagues, and it shows later in the day
options.C: The afternoon queue is always longer, so there is less time between each contact
options.D: Each hard contact triggers a stress response, and without recovery you carry it into the next

questions.stem: A customer has just raised their voice at you for six minutes. The next contact is waiting, and you have about thirty seconds. What do you do?

options.A: Tell a colleague about the customer for a few minutes, to get it off your chest before the next one
options.B: Open the next contact at once, to protect your handle time and keep the queue moving
options.C: One physiological sigh, drop your shoulders and jaw, write one line with no customer details, then breathe
options.D: Scroll your phone for a few seconds, to take your mind off the last customer completely

questions.stem: Your bus is late and you will be twelve minutes past your start time. What do you do?

options.A: Message or call your team lead before your start time, with the delay and your arrival time
options.B: Arrive, log in quietly, and explain the delay only if someone on the team asks you about it later
options.C: Ask a colleague to cover your queue for you, without telling the team lead about it
options.D: Skip your first break to make up the twelve minutes, without telling anyone about it

questions.stem: The system is down. A colleague asks you to send a screenshot of a case to their personal email "because I need it for the customer." What do you do?

options.A: Send it, because the colleague needs it urgently to help the customer while the main system is down
options.B: Keep the data in the approved system and point the colleague to the approved route or their manager
options.C: Send it, but remove the customer's street address and phone number from the screenshot first
options.D: Ask the customer for permission on the phone first, and then send it to the colleague

questions.stem: Your team lead asks, "How are things going?" Which answer gives the kind of evidence a team lead remembers?

options.A: "Busy, but good. Lots going on, and I'm keeping on top of my queue every day."
options.B: "I'm really committed to developing here, and I always put the customer first."
options.C: "Steady. I rewrote the return-process note and a few people use it now. Where should I focus next month?"
options.D: "I've had the best quality score on the team. Can I be considered for the next opening?"

questions.stem: A representative has a clear eye for detail, gives feedback that people accept, and has a quality record that holds up. Which of the four paths has exactly this bar?

options.A: Senior representative
options.B: Quality reviewer
options.C: Subject expert
options.D: Team lead

questions.stem: You want your results to be visible without bragging. Which of these does that?

options.A: "I have had the best quality score on the whole team for three months running, by quite a margin."
options.B: Keep your results to yourself, so that you do not look arrogant in front of the team
options.C: "I would like a promotion, and I will keep asking every quarter until I get one."
options.D: "Since I started using the three-line case note, my contacts don't come back. I've written it up for the team."

questions.stem: A promotion you asked for went to someone else. What do you say to your team lead?

options.A: "Thank you for telling me. I'm disappointed, and I want to use this well. What would make the difference next time?"
options.B: "I understand, but my numbers were better than theirs, so I'd like to know how it was decided."
options.C: Say nothing, hide the disappointment, and do not raise the promotion with your team lead again
options.D: "Can I be considered first for the next opening, since I missed out this time?"

questions.stem: Past the first months in the job, what does the course say "good" now means?

options.A: Every call is answered politely, kept as short as possible, and closed without any transfer to another team.
options.B: Handle time is the lowest on the team, and every call ends inside the target the employer has set for it.
options.C: The problem is actually solved, the next person can pick up the case, and performance is steady.
options.D: One or two outstanding calls each week that the team leader can use as an example for the other agents.

questions.stem: What does the stranger test check?

options.A: Whether a stranger could continue the case from your note without calling you.
options.B: Whether a customer who has never called before can understand the opening of your call.
options.C: Whether an assessor who does not know you would give the call full marks on every criterion.
options.D: Whether a new agent could repeat your call word for word after reading your note once.

questions.stem: In what order are the four behaviors of the First-Contact Standard used?

options.A: Relevance, Low Threat, Curiosity, Autonomy.
options.B: Low Threat, Autonomy, Relevance, Curiosity.
options.C: Curiosity, Relevance, Autonomy, Low Threat.
options.D: Autonomy, Curiosity, Low Threat, Relevance.

questions.stem: A customer says, "I've called twice about this replacement and nothing has moved." Which reply follows A.R.T.?

options.A: "I understand you're frustrated, but the dispatch team is very busy at this time of year."
options.B: "That delay is the courier's fault, not ours. Would you like me to log a complaint for you?"
options.C: "I'm so sorry about that. I promise it will arrive tomorrow. Is that all right with you?"
options.D: "You're frustrated: you've called twice and nothing moved. I can get you a confirmed time and a written update today. What would help most right now, me chasing the case today or an update you can forward?"

questions.stem: You know your handle-time target. What else must you read before you start working on the number?

options.A: The handle time of the fastest agent on your team, so that you know what figure to aim for.
options.B: The reason your employer chose that measure, so that you can decide whether you agree with it.
options.C: Yesterday's figure only, since a single day is the clearest guide to how you are doing.
options.D: The definition and the period: what the measure counts and over what time.

questions.stem: Across five days an agent's handle time is flat at about five minutes, except for one long call on a billing dispute that was resolved with no callback. How should the agent read the week?

options.A: The trend is flat; the spike was one complex case, not a habit.
options.B: The week was poor, because one long call shows the agent is losing control of handle time.
options.C: The long call should be hidden from the record, so that the weekly average looks normal.
options.D: The agent should shorten every call next week to make up for the time lost on that one.

questions.stem: Which measure does the course say depends mostly on you rather than on the customer?

options.A: First contact resolution.
options.B: Customer satisfaction.
options.C: Adherence.
options.D: The number of repeat callers.

questions.stem: You believe two repeat contacts were wrongly counted against your first contact resolution. What do you say to your team leader?

options.A: "My resolution figure looks bad this week, but those callbacks were not my fault. Can you fix it?"
options.B: "I have three call notes where the customer came back about a separate issue, and the notes show the first contact was closed. What would you need from me to look at how those were counted?"
options.C: "Other agents had the same callbacks and their figures were not marked down. Why were mine?"
options.D: "I remember those calls well, and I am sure they were closed. Please remove them from my record."

questions.stem: What is a warm transfer?

options.A: Telling the caller politely which team they need, apologizing for the wait, and then placing the call in that team's queue.
options.B: Staying on the line and briefing the next team with the caller's name, verified account, issue and what you already tried.
options.C: Asking the caller to explain the issue again to the next agent while you stay on the line and listen.
options.D: Sending the next team a written note about the case after the caller has already been put through.

questions.stem: In a warm transfer, what is the correct order?

options.A: Introduce the caller first, let the caller explain, then brief the agent.
options.B: Leave as soon as the agent answers, then send the briefing in a note.
options.C: Brief the caller on the next team's process, then leave before the agent joins.
options.D: Brief the agent first, then introduce the caller, then leave.

questions.stem: A caller asks about a charge. You check and find you can correct it yourself with the tools you have. What should you do?

options.A: Transfer the caller to billing anyway, since billing is the team that normally deals with charges.
options.B: Ask the caller, "Would you like me to put you through to billing?" and follow their answer.
options.C: Resolve it yourself; an avoidable transfer adds a step for the caller.
options.D: Transfer the caller without a briefing, so that your own handle time stays inside the target.

questions.stem: The same caller rings back about the same delivery issue. How should you open?

options.A: "I have your call from the ninth about the delivery date. What is still open?"
options.B: "Could you start from the beginning and tell me what the problem is, please?"
options.C: "I can see you've called us before. Why are you calling again about this one?"
options.D: "I'm sorry, but I wasn't the agent who took your first call about the delivery."

questions.stem: On a live call the customer asks something you do not know. What is the first step?

options.A: Name the delay out loud and honestly before you pull in help.
options.B: Give your best guess, so that the customer is not kept waiting for an answer.
options.C: Stay silent on the line while you search, so that the customer is not disturbed.
options.D: Ask the customer to call back later, when you have had time to find the answer.

questions.stem: Your team leader says you gave an answer before verifying the account. Which response follows the course?

options.A: "I only did that once, and the customer was in a hurry. Is it really that serious?"
options.B: "I'll try to be better at openings from now on. Thanks for letting me know about it."
options.C: "You observed I gave the answer before I verified the account. I'll verify first on every call this week and tell you at our next one-to-one. What would you need to see to know it's fixed?"
options.D: "Why was that call picked for review? Most of my calls this week went very well."

questions.stem: A peer has skipped the same verification step on several calls. How should you raise it with them?

options.A: By telling them plainly that they keep skipping the step and that they need to stop doing it.
options.B: By mentioning it to other colleagues first, so that the peer hears about it from the team.
options.C: By asking them why they keep missing the step, so that they explain themselves properly.
options.D: With dates and facts only, no guess about the reason, and a how or what question at the end.

questions.stem: At shift change, a detail in your open case could not be verified before you finish. What goes in the handover note?

options.A: Nothing about it, so that the next agent does not think less of your work on the case.
options.B: A plain line saying it was not verified.
options.C: A line saying the detail was verified, with a reminder to yourself to check it tomorrow.
options.D: A general line such as "customer called, advised", so that the note stays short and quick.

questions.stem: How does the course say you catch a repeating error in your own queue?

options.A: Wait for the monthly report from your team leader, because only a formal report can show a real pattern.
options.B: Ask customers on each call whether they have had the same problem with us before.
options.C: Rely on memory during the shift, since a busy agent notices patterns automatically.
options.D: Take one deliberate pause at the end of a shift and ask what you saw more than once.

questions.stem: You think the intake form is causing the same repeat on many calls. What turns that hunch into a case someone can act on?

options.A: A strong message to your team leader explaining how frustrating the problem has become.
options.B: A sample of your own six-part notes that shows the pattern.
options.C: The agreement of several colleagues that they have noticed the same thing on their calls.
options.D: Your memory of the calls this week, described to your team leader in as much detail as you can.

questions.stem: You find a repeating gap is partly caused by your own thin notes and partly by a form you do not control. What do you do?

options.A: Fix your own part today, and raise the systemic part with a record attached.
options.B: Wait for the process owner to fix the form before you change anything in your own notes.
options.C: Fix the form yourself by telling callers what to expect, and say nothing more about it.
options.D: Treat the whole gap as the system's fault, since the form was the original cause of it.

questions.stem: When you raise the gap with your team leader, which closing line keeps your ask inside your authority?

options.A: "Someone needs to fix this system before it costs the team any more time."
options.B: "I've told callers the form will be changed soon. Can you make that happen?"
options.C: "What would it take to test adding the order-number field at intake for two weeks?"
options.D: "I've decided to stop using the intake form on my calls until it is corrected."

questions.stem: When you escalate an angry caller, in what order does the supervisor need the information?

options.A: The caller's mood, then your own view of the caller, then the full history of the account.
options.B: An apology for escalating, then the caller's demand, then a request to take the call over.
options.C: The facts, then the caller's state in one line, then one clear ask.
options.D: One clear ask, then the reason you could not solve it, then the facts if there is time.

questions.stem: Which three parts make up the three-part no?

options.A: Apologize for the policy, explain the limit several times, and offer to make an exception.
options.B: State the limit firmly, give all the reasons for it, and ask whether the caller accepts it.
options.C: Acknowledge the caller's anger, promise to try, and transfer the caller to a supervisor.
options.D: Acknowledge the request as reasonable, state the limit once, and offer the real path.

questions.stem: A caller says, "Get me your manager." Which reply follows the course?

options.A: "You want this decided by someone above me, and I understand that. Let me prepare the case so they get it complete the first time. What would you want decided first?"
options.B: "My manager is not available right now, so I'm afraid there is nothing more I can do."
options.C: "I'll get my manager, and I'm sure they will remove the charge for you today."
options.D: "There is no need for a manager. Why don't you let me explain it one more time?"

questions.stem: When does the course say to escalate a case?

options.A: After you have tried at least four different explanations and the caller still does not accept them.
options.B: As soon as you can see it needs authority you do not have, with a recommendation attached.
options.C: Only when the caller raises their voice or asks for a manager more than once on the same call.
options.D: At the end of the shift, so that the supervisor can review all the day's hard cases together.

questions.stem: Which three parts make a callback promise you can keep?

options.A: A sincere apology, a general time such as "later today", and a promise that the answer will be good news.
options.B: A specific time or window, what you will bring back, and what happens if you cannot reach them.
options.C: The name of your team leader, the reference number, and a promise that someone will call back soon.
options.D: A time that suits your shift, a second number for you, and a request that the customer stay by the phone.

questions.stem: You call back at the promised time and nobody answers. What should you do?

options.A: Try again at a different time of day, leave a message with a real next step, and update the note.
options.B: Call several more times within the same hour, so that the customer sees how hard you tried to reach them.
options.C: Close the case with the line "customer did not answer", since the promised callback was made on time.
options.D: Leave a long, apologetic message that explains the full case and all the account details in it.

questions.stem: You reach a customer two hours after the time you promised. How should you open?

options.A: With a long apology that explains how busy the queue has been since this morning.
options.B: Without mentioning the time at all, so that the customer's attention stays on the answer.
options.C: By asking, "Is now still a good time, or have you already sorted this out elsewhere?"
options.D: "I promised to call you by two o'clock and I missed it." Say it plainly, then move to what you have for them.

questions.stem: You call a business customer and the person who answers may not own the issue. What should your first question do?

options.A: Explain the whole case to the person who answered, so that they can pass it on.
options.B: Ask why nobody in their team has dealt with the issue before now.
options.C: Find out who in their team owns this kind of issue.
options.D: Confirm whether this person is willing to take a decision on behalf of the owner.

questions.stem: According to the course, which part of a quality scorecard is the least useful to you?

options.A: The overall number.
options.B: The individual criteria and their scores.
options.C: The assessor's notes on specific moments.
options.D: The pattern across your last three reviews.

questions.stem: You lose marks on the same criterion in three reviews in a row. How should you read that?

options.A: As a bad sample each time, since any single review can catch an unusual call.
options.B: As proof that the assessor is applying the criterion unfairly to your calls.
options.C: As a sign that the overall score matters more than any one criterion does.
options.D: As a pattern, which is what coaching is for.

questions.stem: You believe a mark on the verification step is wrong. What do you ask for first?

options.A: The outcome: "Can you change this score, please? I did verify the account."
options.B: The standard: "What would full marks have sounded like on the verification step?"
options.C: The reason: "Why did the assessor mark me down when I followed the process?"
options.D: A second opinion from a colleague on your team who heard part of the call from the next desk.

questions.stem: A review marks you down on the opening, a policy explanation and the wrap-up. What does the course say to do next?

options.A: Work on all three at once, so that the next review shows improvement on every criterion.
options.B: Wait for the next review to see whether the same three criteria are marked down again.
options.C: Choose one change, make it specific enough to hear on the next call, and check it against your notes.
options.D: Send the team leader a message the same evening explaining why the review felt unfair after such a hard week.

questions.stem: The course says your job stands on four legs. Which four?

options.A: Speed, sales, product knowledge and popularity with the team.
options.B: Handle time, overtime, call volume and length of service.
options.C: Attendance, appearance, typing speed and friendliness on calls.
options.D: Schedule, attendance, notes and conduct.

questions.stem: During a reset after a hostile call, which wording does the course recommend for naming what happened?

options.A: "That customer was awful."
options.B: "I always get the worst callers."
options.C: "That call was hard."
options.D: "I should never have taken that call."

questions.stem: In the 90-day plan, what are weeks 1 to 2 for?

options.A: Looking outward: choosing one skill to strengthen and one working relationship to build.
options.B: Stabilizing the routine: one reset habit, one note habit and one recovery habit, held daily.
options.C: Building the buffer: noticing where your energy drops and adjusting breaks and tasks.
options.D: Asking for promotion: collecting evidence and booking a meeting with the team leader.

questions.stem: You have been late for two of your last four shifts and nobody has raised it yet. What does the course advise?

options.A: Raise it yourself with the facts: "I have been late on two of my last four shifts, and I want to tell you before it looks bigger than it is. What would help you see this turning around?"
options.B: Say nothing and make sure you are on time from now on, so that it is forgotten.
options.C: Tell your team leader, "I might be in trouble with my attendance. Is that okay?"
options.D: Wait until it is raised formally, then explain the reasons for each late start in detail.

questions.stem: Which four kinds of evidence make a credible case for promotion?

options.A: Length of service, a clean record with no real problems, being liked by the team, and saying that you are ready.
options.B: Your own numbers as trends, hard cases handled well, cross-team work you led, and reviews that show growth.
options.C: Your single best week, praise from customers, the hours of overtime worked, and your team leader's opinion.
options.D: A high overall quality score, low handle time, perfect attendance, and the number of calls taken each day.

questions.stem: An agent's resolution figure dipped in month two and recovered in month three. Which figures should the case show?

options.A: Month three only, because the most recent month is the one a decision maker cares about.
options.B: Months one and three, leaving out the dip so that the record looks steady throughout.
options.C: All three months, because a dip that recovered shows the agent notices and adjusts.
options.D: The best single week from each month, so that the strongest results stand out clearly.

questions.stem: Your team leader asks why you should be considered for a senior agent role. Which answer follows the course?

options.A: "I'd like to be considered for the senior agent role. I have three months of my own figures, two hard cases I carried with another team, and two reviews where a noted weakness became a strength. What would you need to see from me to support that in the next round?"
options.B: "I've been here over a year now and I've never had a real problem. I think I'm ready for the next step."
options.C: "I work harder than most people on this team. Will you put my name forward for the role this month?"
options.D: "Everyone on the team says I should go for it. Can you tell me today whether I will get the role?"

questions.stem: When the four-line shape is used internally to ask for a next step, what do the four lines cover?

options.A: How long you have worked there, why you deserve the role, who supports you, and when you expect an answer.
options.B: Your best call, your best review, your best week, and a request for a decision by the end of the month.
options.C: An apology for asking, a list of your strengths, a list of your weaknesses, and a thank-you for the time.
options.D: What you are asking for, what you are bringing, when you would like to discuss it, and a reference you can both find.

questions.stem: A new team leader spends the whole day with the team. Their manager only hears from them when something has already gone wrong. Which habit does the course say belongs in the "up to your manager" direction?

options.A: Keep the manager out of team problems until they are fully solved
options.B: Send a full weekly report on every task, whether or not anything changed
options.C: Give honest updates, raise problems early and bring proposals, not only complaints
options.D: Ask the manager to step in and solve problems directly with the team

questions.stem: In a one-to-one, a leader asks what is happening with the work, then what makes it hard. Next they ask, "What would help most right now?" Which rung of The Question Ladder did they skip?

options.A: Impact
options.B: Situation
options.C: Need
options.D: Problem

questions.stem: You give a colleague a three-part expectation for running next week's huddle. Which step does the course say catches most misunderstandings?

options.A: Repeating the expectation twice, a little louder the second time
options.B: Sending the expectation in writing after the conversation ends
options.C: Asking at the end, "Is that clear?" and waiting for a yes
options.D: The person saying the expectation back in their own words

questions.stem: When does the course say you should use A.R.T.?

options.A: When planning the week's tasks with the team at the huddle
options.B: When a concern, resistance or complaint blocks the conversation
options.C: When reviewing your notes after a one-to-one with a team member
options.D: When setting a new task with a clear deadline for someone

questions.stem: Which of these is a leading number?

options.A: Revenue booked by the team last month
options.B: Follow-up calls made within a day of the first contact
options.C: Complaints closed by the team across the whole last quarter
options.D: Total orders placed by customers last week

questions.stem: Your manager wants your team held to a measure that depends mostly on another department's backlog. Which of the three questions before you trust a number flags the problem?

options.A: What exactly does it count?
options.B: What does it leave out?
options.C: How does it compare with other teams?
options.D: Who controls it?

questions.stem: Your team hits its monthly figure with a strong finish, but the return rate after purchase doubles. What does the course say a leader should do?

options.A: Ask what was different in how the results were reached
options.B: Praise the team for the figure and treat the returns separately
options.C: Raise next month's target, since the team has shown it can do more
options.D: Remove the return rate from the scorecard so it does not distract

questions.stem: Your daily huddle has grown to 25 minutes because the team analyzes every bad number in detail. What fits the course?

options.A: Cancel the huddle and send the numbers by email instead
options.B: Keep the long analysis, since it shows the team is engaged with the numbers
options.C: Show the scoreboard and today's focus briefly, and take problems offline
options.D: Hold the huddle only on days when the numbers look good

questions.stem: A leader keeps moving a team member's one-to-one whenever something routine comes up. What does the course say happens?

options.A: The team member gets more time to prepare and brings a better agenda each week
options.B: The leader gains time for the work that matters most that week
options.C: Nothing changes, as long as the meeting happens at some point
options.D: The slot stops being reliable and the team member treats it as optional

questions.stem: In a development one-to-one, which question fits the Impact rung of The Question Ladder?

options.A: "What part of the job gives you energy?"
options.B: "What do the next six months look like if the work stays as it is?"
options.C: "What would the first step be, and when exactly could you take it this week?"
options.D: "What makes it hard to get there right now?"

questions.stem: A new team member is three weeks into the role and still unsure of several basics. How does the course say to coach them?

options.A: Give them a stretch task just beyond the job so they grow faster
options.B: List all five areas they need to fix so they know where they stand
options.C: Build: ask what feels unclear, then agree one small, specific step
options.D: Leave them to learn by watching until they ask for help themselves

questions.stem: A team member describes clearly which part of a task is hard, but still cannot get the result. What kind of gap is this most likely to be, and what is the fix?

options.A: A skill gap: teaching, demonstration or a smaller task to practice
options.B: A motivation gap: reconnect the task to why it matters for the team and customers
options.C: A motivation gap: remove an obstacle and offer support this week
options.D: A skill gap: set a firmer deadline so the person takes it seriously

questions.stem: Which of these delegates a decision, not only a task?

options.A: "You decide refunds up to the standard limit; anything above it comes to me first."
options.B: "Please order the standard parts for the vans this week and let me know when it is done."
options.C: "Run the report for me today and send it to me before you leave."
options.D: "Check with me each time a customer asks, it is quicker that way."

questions.stem: A leader briefs a handover with the task and why, what done looks like, and a dated check-in. The team member now checks in with every small question. Which part of the four-part briefing was missing?

options.A: A second dated check-in a week later
options.B: A longer explanation of why the task matters
options.C: The limits of the person's decisions
options.D: A written copy of what done looks like

questions.stem: You name a buddy to support a new team member for the first two weeks. Which limit does the course give the buddy?

options.A: The buddy assesses performance and reports on it at the end of week two
options.B: The buddy guides and answers questions, but does not assess performance or promise pay, hours or title
options.C: The buddy decides the new person's schedule and sets their first targets
options.D: The buddy takes over the leader's one-to-ones with the new person

questions.stem: Two team members always get the interesting work, the praise and the flexibility. The rest of the team has quietly disengaged. Which pattern from field practice is this?

options.A: Buddy
options.B: Ghost
options.C: Hero
options.D: Favorite

questions.stem: What turns SBI from a description into development?

options.A: Repeating the Impact part until the person agrees with it
options.B: Adding a comment on the person's attitude so the point is clear
options.C: Agreeing what the person will do differently and how they will practice it, with a date
options.D: Sending the full feedback in writing afterwards, so there is a clear record of what was said

questions.stem: Your strongest performer is curt with colleagues, and a newer colleague now avoids the morning call. How does the course say to open the feedback?

options.A: Start with their sales figures, then mention the behavior briefly
options.B: Tell them they have a bad attitude that the whole team has noticed
options.C: Wait for a quieter month so the conversation does not hurt this month's results
options.D: Use SBI on the behavior toward colleagues, with the numbers left out

questions.stem: You give feedback to a former peer, who replies, "So we are not friends anymore?" Which line is the Acknowledge step of A.R.T.?

options.A: "I understand, but work is work and this has to change."
options.B: "It sounds like my comment feels like it changes something between us."
options.C: "Why would you take a work comment so personally?"
options.D: "I can see you are upset about this, but we still need to talk about the lateness."
