questions.stem: You ask your team for feedback on your own leadership. One person says your late changes to the rota make planning hard. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Say back what you heard and name one thing you will change, without defending
options.B: Explain the reasons behind the late rota changes so the person understands the pressure
options.C: Thank them, note it down, and review it with the others at year end
options.D: Ask the rest of the team whether they agree before you respond

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the five-step underperformance conversation?

options.A: Ask then listen, name the gap, agree three changes, warn, follow through
options.B: Name the gap with facts using SBI, ask then listen, agree one change, agree a dated check-in, follow through
options.C: Agree a dated check-in, name the gap, give advice, agree one change, follow through
options.D: Name the gap, explain the rules, agree a plan with six points, check in if needed, close

questions.stem: A leader gives a team member feedback twice about missed afternoon callbacks, but never checks back. What does the course say the team learns?

options.A: That feedback is a conversation, not a standard
options.B: That the leader trusts them to fix it on their own
options.C: That callbacks matter more than other tasks on the shift
options.D: That the next step will be a formal warning from HR

questions.stem: A gap has survived a good SBI conversation, and you suspect the person simply does not care. What does the course say to do before you decide the cause?

options.A: Tell the person you have noticed their lack of effort and expect a clear change this week
options.B: Ask, "Why do you keep missing this?" so they explain themselves
options.C: Treat it as a motivation problem, since that is the most common cause
options.D: Climb The Question Ladder with how and what questions to find the real cause

questions.stem: After a third conversation, a team member asks what happens next. Which reply fits the course?

options.A: "You will probably get a written warning, so be ready for that."
options.B: "Do not worry, nothing formal will happen to you this time."
options.C: "I will check with HR and come back to you by Thursday."
options.D: "That depends on you, so you already know the answer to that."

questions.stem: Two team members clash for the third time over handovers. Why does the course say to talk to each person privately first?

options.A: So you can hear both versions and decide who is right before you bring them together
options.B: So each person can put a formal complaint on record about the other
options.C: So you can collect notes on each person for a possible file later
options.D: Without an audience there is less face to protect, and people say what is going on

questions.stem: Which agreement at the end of a joint conversation is most likely to hold?

options.A: "From now on, you will both be more careful with handovers."
options.B: "The late-shift leaver writes three handover lines before logging off, and the opener reads them before the first call, from Monday."
options.C: "Let us all try to be more professional with each other."
options.D: "I trust you both to sort this out between yourselves now."

questions.stem: In a joint conversation, how does the course say to run the Acknowledge step of A.R.T.?

options.A: Acknowledge each side out loud before you respond to either
options.B: Acknowledge the person who raised the issue first, then move on
options.C: Acknowledge the side with the stronger case, so the other side adjusts
options.D: Skip Acknowledge, because both people already know how they feel

questions.stem: You have written a new standard with the two people who kept colliding. What does the course say makes it stick?

options.A: It is posted on the wall and signed by both people involved
options.B: It applies only to the two people who had the conflict
options.C: It is specific, the same for everyone, modeled by you first and followed up
options.D: It comes with a clear warning about what happens if either person breaks it again

questions.stem: A team member says, "The old system worked fine." According to the course, what helps them most to start moving with the change?

options.A: Naming what stays the same, which restores a sense of control
options.B: Repeating the decision more firmly so there is no doubt about it
options.C: Explaining that head office decided it and nothing can be done
options.D: Pointing out that the rest of the team has already accepted it

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the four-part change announcement?

options.A: The why, the decision, what happens next, what is fixed versus open
options.B: What happens next, the decision, the why, what is fixed versus open
options.C: The decision, the why, what is fixed versus open, what happens next
options.D: What is fixed versus open, the why, the decision, what happens next

questions.stem: A team member pushes back on a new process. You want to reframe with a number, but you have no data behind it. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Use a likely figure anyway, since a number makes the reframe sound stronger
options.B: Promise that the process will save time, so the person relaxes
options.C: Skip Reframe and go straight to a yes/no question to close it
options.D: Say what you do know and leave the rest open; use verified facts only

questions.stem: During a busy week a team member did excellent work, and you know they find public praise uncomfortable. Which recognition fits all four tests?

options.A: Praise them in front of the whole team at the next huddle, so others see it
options.B: A private message today naming what they did and what it saved the team
options.C: A general thank-you to the whole team for a good, hard week
options.D: A note to raise their work at the quarterly review when it is calmer

questions.stem: Response time has slipped and you cannot approve extra hours yourself. Which update fits the course?

options.A: "It has been busy, but I think we are getting on top of it."
options.B: "Response time moved to two days because of a vacancy. I cannot approve extra hours. I recommend borrowing one person for ten days, starting Monday."
options.C: "I will let you know once I have fixed it, so you do not need to worry."
options.D: "Response time slipped. What do you want me to do about it?"

questions.stem: You bring your manager a proposal. Which set of parts does the course list?

options.A: The problem, who caused it, what it cost, and who should fix it
options.B: A full report of the month, the team's feelings, and a request for help
options.C: Your opinion, the team's opinion, and a vote on what to do next
options.D: What to change, why it matters, what it costs or risks, and your first step and return date

questions.stem: Another department keeps sending a weekly report late, and pressing harder only makes them defend their own numbers. What does the course say is usually underneath this friction?

options.A: The other department does not respect your team's work
options.B: The other team leader is avoiding you on purpose
options.C: Each department is measured on something different
options.D: Your manager has not given you enough authority

questions.stem: A leader waits to report a problem until it is fixed, so the update looks tidy. What does the course say this costs?

options.A: It removes the manager's chance to help, and if the fix fails they hear late
options.B: It makes the leader look too dependent on the manager
options.C: It slows the fix down, because the manager will then ask for many more reports
options.D: Nothing, as long as the fix works in the end

questions.stem: What three columns does the course suggest for your leadership record?

options.A: Goal, effort, feeling
options.B: Team member, mistake, warning
options.C: Date, situation, result or behavior
options.D: Task, hours, sign-off

questions.stem: Why does the course say your record should include a result that did not go well, with what you changed?

options.A: A record with only wins reads as a highlight reel, and sensible managers discount it
options.B: It shows you are modest and self-aware, which managers value in any candidate for promotion
options.C: It gives your manager a reason to offer you more training before promotion
options.D: It protects you if a team member later complains about that result

questions.stem: You start cross-training a senior team member on some of your decisions. What does the course say to tell them?

options.A: Nothing yet, so they do not expect a promotion from it
options.B: That you are training them on these decisions because they are ready, and it makes the team stronger
options.C: That they will take over your role once you are promoted
options.D: That it is a test, and their results will decide their next review

questions.stem: You present your promotion case to your manager. Which closing line fits the course?

options.A: "Do you think I am ready for a promotion?"
options.B: "I have worked really hard, so can we talk about my promotion?"
options.C: "Would you be willing to promote me this year?"
options.D: "What would you need to see from me over the next two quarters to be considered?"

questions.stem: A team member asks you for an extra day off next week. Approving it sits above your authority. Which reply fits the middle position as the course teaches it?

options.A: "Leave it with me, I am fairly sure I can get that through for you."
options.B: "I cannot approve that myself. I will take it to the manager today and tell you by Friday."
options.C: "Yes, take it. I will explain it to the manager when they are back next week."
options.D: "That is not something I deal with, so you will need to ask someone else about it."

questions.stem: What does the Reframe step of A.R.T. do?

options.A: It explains the rule again, more clearly, so the person understands why it exists
options.B: It offers the person something in return if they accept what you are asking
options.C: It defends your own position so the person sees you had a good reason
options.D: It shifts the criterion to what changing it would cost or protect for the team

questions.stem: Which four parts make up the four-part expectation from Day 1?

options.A: Result, time, who depends on it, and what to do if it slips
options.B: Outcome, steps, deadline, and checkpoints along the way
options.C: Task, reason, reward, and the consequence for the team if it is missed
options.D: Goal, owner, budget, and a weekly report on progress

questions.stem: A team member asks you to change their contracted hours from next month. How should you sort this decision?

options.A: Own it: agree the change yourself, since you know the rota and the busy days better than anyone
options.B: Document it only: note the request and wait to see if it comes up again
options.C: Escalate it early, with a recommendation attached, because hours sit above your authority
options.D: Own it for now and tell the manager only if the team member complains

questions.stem: Your manager tracks one sales figure. According to the course, what should you read next to it?

options.A: The activity that should produce it, and one number that would reveal corner-cutting
options.B: The same sales figure from other stores and other employers, so you can see how the team compares
options.C: A longer list of every figure the business tracks, all given equal weight
options.D: Nothing else, because one clear number keeps the team focused on the target

questions.stem: You trace a disappointing result through each stage, from enquiry to purchase. What should you compare each stage's drop against?

options.A: An industry standard published for your sector
options.B: The figures another branch shared with you at the area meeting last month
options.C: Your own team's history, since definitions vary by employer
options.D: The target your manager set for the whole year

questions.stem: Which line belongs in your daily record?

options.A: "The late shift seemed lazy today and did not try very hard with customers."
options.B: "One team member had family problems again, so the numbers were bad."
options.C: "Quiet day overall, nothing much to report, should pick up next week."
options.D: "Tuesday: two team members absent, contact rate dropped, cover arranged."

questions.stem: Your team missed its weekly target and your manager asks what happened. Which answer fits the course?

options.A: "It was a quiet week, footfall was down, and the team did their best. It will pick up."
options.B: "Two absences on our busiest days cut contact; conversion held. Fix: cover agreed by Thursday. What would you want to see next update?"
options.C: "Honestly, the target was set too high for this time of year, so we were never going to hit it."
options.D: "I am not sure yet. Can you tell me what you would like me to change next week?"

questions.stem: In urgent versus important sorting, what happens to a task that is important but not urgent?

options.A: It is done first, before anything else on the list
options.B: It is delegated or done in a ten-minute batch
options.C: It gets a block in your day
options.D: It is dropped, because it is usually no job at all

questions.stem: A team member calls in sick for the late shift. In what order does the course say to arrange cover?

options.A: Check if the shift can run at a reduced standard you can name, then ask for a voluntary swap, then use your own authority
options.B: Use your own authority to move someone, then ask for a swap, then check whether the shift can run short
options.C: Cover the gap yourself first, then ask for a swap if you get tired later in the shift
options.D: Message the whole group asking if someone can cover, then wait to see who replies

questions.stem: Cover for tomorrow needs a decision above your authority. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Wait until the end of the day, when the manager has more time to read it
options.B: Send a written request the same morning with the shift, the gap, the options and your recommendation
options.C: Tell the team that cover is confirmed, then ask the manager to approve it later
options.D: Leave the gap open and see whether the shift manages without anyone extra

questions.stem: What single habit does the course say changes the tone of the daily huddle?

options.A: Reading every number from the weekly report out loud to the team
options.B: Letting each person speak for as long as they need to
options.C: Holding the huddle only on days when there is a problem to solve
options.D: Ending every item with an owner and a deadline

questions.stem: What is the course's test of whether a standard is ready?

options.A: Your manager has signed it off and it is filed with the store records
options.B: The team has agreed to it at the huddle, and no one objected when it was read out
options.C: It uses the same wording as the standard in the employer's handbook
options.D: A person walking in for the first time could check it without asking you

questions.stem: A new team member needs a checklist beside them for the first weeks to meet the closing standard. How does the course describe this?

options.A: An exemption: new people meet a lighter standard until they settle in
options.B: A support, not an exemption: the standard is the same, the help changes with experience
options.C: A risk: other team members will expect the same checklist and lower the standard
options.D: A favor that should stay private so the rest of the team does not notice

questions.stem: A team member tells you the temperature log was missed on Tuesday. How does the course say to respond?

options.A: Note the person's name in the record so the pattern is clear at the next audit
options.B: Remind them that missed logs are serious and must not happen again on any shift they run
options.C: Thank them, ask what would prevent it next time, and tell the team what you changed
options.D: Say nothing for now and check whether it happens again before acting on it

questions.stem: What are the four parts of the four-part brief from Day 4?

options.A: Outcome, steps, deadline, checkpoints
options.B: Result, time, who depends on it, what if it slips
options.C: Situation, behavior, impact, practice
options.D: Problem, impact, options, recommendation

questions.stem: How should a fifteen-minute one-to-one end?

options.A: With a summary of everything discussed, read back by the assistant manager
options.B: With one agreement: one behavior, one date, one check
options.C: With a list of goals for the person to work through over the month
options.D: With a yes/no question such as "Are you happy with that?"

questions.stem: Why does the course say "For the next three shifts, offer the second product first" works better than "Be more proactive"?

options.A: A specific practice needs no extra thinking, while an abstract idea competes for limited attention
options.B: A longer instruction sounds more serious and more official, so the person is more likely to take it on board
options.C: Naming a product shows the person that the manager knows the range better than they do
options.D: A short request is easier to forget, so the person feels less pressure afterwards

questions.stem: Which part of SBI feedback does the course say most people skip?

options.A: Situation: saying when and where it happened
options.B: Behavior: describing what the person actually did
options.C: Impact: naming what it caused for others
options.D: Practice: what the person will try next, and when you will look

questions.stem: You hand a team member a task with several moving parts. What does the course say to agree out loud at handover?

options.A: That they should only contact you if something goes badly wrong
options.B: That you will take the task back if it is not done by Friday
options.C: The follow-up rhythm, such as an update after the first call, then daily until Friday
options.D: A reward for finishing early, so they stay motivated all week

questions.stem: A team member pushes back on a new end-of-shift check. Which line is the Acknowledge step as the course teaches it?

options.A: "I can see this is frustrating for you, and honestly that feels completely fair to me."
options.B: "I understand, but the check is not optional for anyone on the team."
options.C: "It sounds like this check feels like extra work with no payoff for you."
options.D: "Why does one short check at the end of a shift bother you so much?"

questions.stem: You now set the rota for a former peer who is also a friend. What does the course say about holding the standard with them?

options.A: Relax the standard a little at first, so the friendship can adjust slowly
options.B: Hold them to a stricter standard than others, so nobody can accuse you of favoritism
options.C: Avoid the topic and let them notice the change on their own over time
options.D: Say the line once, in private, while calm, then never bend it or stiffen it for them

questions.stem: A team member's gap has repeated after A.R.T. and SBI, and employer policy now applies. What does the course say you do?

options.A: Take the matter to your manager or HR with your recommendation
options.B: Issue a formal warning yourself, so the person knows it is serious
options.C: Hint that their hours may be cut if things do not change soon
options.D: Keep handling it yourself, so the record stays out of HR's hands

questions.stem: Why does the course say the same direct sentence can sound like care from one assistant manager and an attack from another?

options.A: Because some people are naturally better speakers and choose softer words
options.B: Because the team reads it against the credit built up in the trust account
options.C: Because a direct sentence always sounds harsh unless it is said in writing
options.D: Because the team only listens to people who have the title of manager

questions.stem: A customer's repair was not ready at the agreed time. Which of these is a fact, not an assumption?

options.A: The receipt shows the repair was booked for collection at ten
options.B: The customer is mainly angry about the money they have lost on the job today
options.C: The customer wants a full refund, not the repair itself
options.D: This is the same complaint the customer made last week

questions.stem: What shape does the course give for the one-sentence problem?

options.A: What the policy says, what the customer did, and what you cannot do
options.B: When it happened, which colleague caused it, and what they should do
options.C: Who is affected, what went wrong, and what is at stake for them
options.D: How the customer feels, what they want, and how much it will cost

questions.stem: In A.R.T. with a customer, what does the course say the Reframe should move toward?

options.A: The company's policy, explained clearly and calmly so the customer accepts it
options.B: What solving it protects for the customer, often their own operation
options.C: A small discount offered in return for the customer's patience
options.D: The reasons the workshop or the team fell behind this week

questions.stem: What is the order of the five-line escalation?

options.A: Impact, problem, ask, options, recommendation
options.B: Problem, options, ask, impact, recommendation
options.C: Recommendation, problem, impact, ask, options
options.D: Problem, impact, options, recommendation, ask

questions.stem: What is the order of the five-part weekly update?

options.A: Numbers, risks, progress, next, decisions needed
options.B: Risks, decisions needed, numbers, progress, next
options.C: Progress, risks, numbers, decisions needed, next
options.D: Progress, numbers, risks, decisions needed, next

questions.stem: It has been a quiet week with little to report. What does the course say about the weekly update?

options.A: Skip it this week and send a longer one next week instead
options.B: Send it at the same time as usual; the rhythm itself is the point
options.C: Send only the risks, since progress and numbers have not moved
options.D: Wait until the manager asks for it, so you do not waste their time

questions.stem: You turn a problem into a proposal for your manager. Which shape does the course give?

options.A: The problem, who caused it, and a request for the manager to decide what to do
options.B: A full history of the issue, every option you considered, and no recommendation
options.C: What is happening and how you know, who it affects and by when, two options, one recommendation, one ask
options.D: A short warning that something is wrong, followed by a meeting request for next week

questions.stem: Your manager says your late stock counts look careless, and you disagree. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Acknowledge how it landed, reframe to what the process protects, then ask a how or what question
options.B: Lay out the facts that prove you were not careless, so the record is corrected
options.C: Agree that you were careless and apologize, so the conversation ends quickly
options.D: Explain your reasons, then ask, "Do you see my point now?"

questions.stem: Your manager is away. A team member asks you to remove a late mark from their formal record. How do you sort this?

options.A: Own it: remove the mark and tell the manager afterward
options.B: Document it only, and decide yourself once the week is over
options.C: Escalate it, because it changes someone's formal record
options.D: Ignore it until the manager is back, without telling anyone

questions.stem: Which three lines does the course use to record a routine decision?

options.A: What you decided, why, and what happens if it goes wrong and what you will do then
options.B: Who asked, what they wanted, and whether you said yes or no to them
options.C: The time, the people who were present, and how each of them felt about the decision
options.D: The rule, the exception you made, and who you will tell about it next week

questions.stem: Your manager is away for a week. What does the course say the daily update should contain?

options.A: A full account of every conversation on the floor that day, so nothing at all is missed
options.B: A short line saying "Everything is fine here", so the manager can relax
options.C: Only problems, since decisions you took yourself do not need reporting
options.D: Decisions you took, what you documented, and what you need, with a recommendation

questions.stem: While your manager is away, a customer demands a refund the policy does not clearly cover. Which reply fits the course?

options.A: "Do not worry, I will sort something out for you today."
options.B: "I can log this and send it to my manager with my recommendation, and answer you by four."
options.C: "Our policy does not cover this, so there is nothing I can do."
options.D: "Can you come back next week when my manager is here?"

questions.stem: What does each line of the commitments list contain?

options.A: The person's name, their attitude, and how reliable you think they are
options.B: What you committed to, the date you gave, the date you finished, and what happened
options.C: The promise, who it pleased, and how it will look to your manager in your next review
options.D: Only the promises you kept, so the list supports your promotion case

questions.stem: What are the four parts of the promotion case?

options.A: Effort, reputation, hours covered, and what colleagues would say about you
options.B: Targets, competitor figures, industry benchmarks, and your salary goal
options.C: Your strengths, your weaknesses, your goals, and a request for a decision
options.D: Numbers, decisions, people, and the successor behind you

questions.stem: Why does the course say naming a successor strengthens your promotion case?

options.A: Your manager asks what breaks behind you, and a named successor shows the move is safe
options.B: It shows your manager that you are ready to leave the team and want to move on as quickly as possible
options.C: It lets you promise the successor your role, so they work harder to support you
options.D: It removes the need to show your own numbers and decisions in the case

questions.stem: If you were offered the Store Manager role, what three parts does the course give for the first 90 days?

options.A: Announce changes, replace weak team members, set new targets
options.B: Fix five problems at once, then review, then rest
options.C: Learn, fix one thing, set the rhythm
options.D: Meet the team, change the rota, raise the targets

questions.stem: The weekly stock count was missed on Friday because two people were off and the delivery came late. Your area manager asks what happened. Which answer shows accountability as the course teaches it?

options.A: "We missed it because two people were off sick, and the delivery came late on top of that."
options.B: "The team did not get to it, but it should be much better this week, I am sure."
options.C: "It was a very hard week for everyone, so the count was the one thing that had to go."
options.D: "We missed the count. I had not named an owner, so I have named one per shift, check next Friday."

questions.stem: What three parts make up a priority line?

options.A: A measurable goal, a named owner and a check date
options.B: A clear reason, a deadline and a reward for the team
options.C: A task, a budget and a weekly report to the area manager
options.D: A target, a team vote and a review at the end of the year

questions.stem: Which of these is an observable expectation for the stockroom?

options.A: "Keep the stockroom tidy, clean and organized at all times, whoever is on shift."
options.B: "Take pride in the stockroom and treat it like your own."
options.C: "Cages emptied by the end of each shift and cardboard flat in the bin."
options.D: "Make sure the stockroom always looks good for visitors."

questions.stem: What is the personal baseline you build on Day 1?

options.A: A list of targets you want the store to reach by the end of the quarter
options.B: A simple record of where your management hours go now, before you change anything
options.C: A summary of each team member's strengths and weaknesses for the year ahead, shared with your manager
options.D: A plan of the changes you will make to the rota in your first month

questions.stem: Sales are up on last month, but margin is down. What does the course say this may tell you?

options.A: The team is performing well, so the same promotion should run again next month as well
options.B: Margin always falls when sales rise, so there is nothing to look into
options.C: The rise may have been bought with discounting, so break down how it was reached
options.D: Wage cost must have risen, so cut hours before the next report comes in

questions.stem: Saturday sales were strong this week. How does the course say to tell whether this is noise or a trend?

options.A: Compare it with the target your area manager set for the month
options.B: Look at the last several periods; one strong Saturday is noise until it repeats
options.C: Ask the team whether it felt busier than a normal Saturday
options.D: Treat it as a trend straight away, so the rota can be changed for next Saturday and the one after

questions.stem: Which of these is a leading number?

options.A: The number of customers who asked for an item you did not have
options.B: Last month's margin as a share of sales, taken from the store's report
options.C: Last quarter's shrink measured at stock count
options.D: Last week's total sales for the store

questions.stem: Why does the course say to read a balanced set of numbers instead of one target figure?

options.A: A longer list of numbers makes the weekly report look more complete and more professional to head office
options.B: One figure is too easy to reach, so the team needs several targets to stay busy
options.C: Area managers only trust reports that show at least ten numbers every week
options.D: When one figure is the target, people move it in ways that damage the lines beside it

questions.stem: Customers complain about queues every Saturday from 11:00 to 14:00, when one floor person is on break. Which fix does the course describe as a rota fix, not a headcount fix?

options.A: Ask the area manager for extra hours on Saturdays
options.B: Move the break before the rush and shift a person from a quiet evening
options.C: Ask the team to work faster during the busy block and take their breaks later in the day
options.D: Close one till so the floor has an extra person

questions.stem: You plan absence and peak cover once a week, before the week starts. Which step does the course include?

options.A: Wait to see who calls in sick, then decide what to drop on the day
options.B: Promise the team that cover will always be found, whatever happens
options.C: Leave cover decisions to whoever opens the store that morning, with no plan
options.D: Name one person who can make the first decision if you are not reachable

questions.stem: The floor feels stretched and you want to ask for more hours. What does the course say to do first?

options.A: Send the request at once, before the budget for the month is used up
options.B: Ask the team to log their own hours for a month so you can show the area manager how hard they work
options.C: Watch one busy block and count what customers wait for, to find the bottleneck
options.D: Compare your hours with a larger store and ask for the same amount

questions.stem: Which four parts does the course give for a case for hours?

options.A: What changed, what it costs, what the customer experiences, the decision you need
options.B: How busy it feels, how tired the team is, what others get, and a request
options.C: Last year's hours, this year's hours, the difference, and a deadline
options.D: The rota, the budget, a list of complaints, and the number of hours

questions.stem: What four parts does the course give for a standard that holds on a bad day?

options.A: One observable behavior, a minimum version, a named checker and a check time
options.B: A clear attitude, a reward, a named checker and a monthly review
options.C: A full written procedure, a training session, a sign-off sheet and an audit date
options.D: A target number, a warning, a deadline and a report to management

questions.stem: Your store keeps losing stock. In what order does the course say to test the likely causes of shrink?

options.A: Theft, process gaps, damage and waste, receiving errors
options.B: Process gaps, theft, receiving errors, damage and waste
options.C: Receiving errors, damage and waste, process gaps, theft
options.D: Damage and waste, theft, receiving errors, process gaps

questions.stem: A team member finds a mismatch between the system and the shelf. What does the course say keeps this kind of reporting alive?

options.A: Asking the team member to explain how the mismatch happened on their shift
options.B: Recording the finder's name so you know who to ask if it happens again
options.C: Waiting until the full count to confirm the mismatch before acting on it
options.D: Acting on the note without blaming the person who found it

questions.stem: Which line is a record someone else can pick up?

options.A: "Someone on the late shift was not checking properly again this week."
options.B: "Evening shift, stock room, three lines short on count, receiving paperwork checked, corrected."
options.C: "Stock problems again. The team needs to be much more careful from now on."
options.D: "Same person on the count as last time, very careless, spoke to them about it."

questions.stem: Which interview question collects evidence, as the course teaches it?

options.A: "Are you good with people?"
options.B: "Tell me about yourself and why you want to work here."
options.C: "How would your friends describe you in three words?"
options.D: "Describe a time a customer was unhappy and you were alone at the front. What did you do?"

questions.stem: A candidate gives a vague answer about handling a difficult customer. What does the course say to do next?

options.A: Move on, since vague answers are common and usually mean nothing
options.B: Ask a how or what follow-up one step deeper, such as "What did you say next?"
options.C: Tell the candidate the answer was weak and ask them to try again
options.D: Give credit anyway if the candidate came across as warm, confident and easy to talk to

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the five onboarding steps?

options.A: Tell, show, learner does while watched, one thing done well plus one to change, check date
options.B: Show, tell, check date, learner does alone, one thing done well plus one to change
options.C: Tell, learner does alone, show, check date, feedback on everything at once
options.D: Show, learner does while watched, tell, check date, one thing to change

questions.stem: Which onboarding step does the course say most managers skip, even though it is the only one that shows what the person understood?

options.A: Tell: explaining the task and the standard in plain words
options.B: Show: demonstrating the task at normal pace, then slowly
options.C: Learner does, while watched
options.D: Check date: agreeing when you will watch again

questions.stem: What are the four parts of delegating an outcome?

options.A: Task, reason, reward, and a review at the end of the month
options.B: Task, standard, check date, and what the owner may decide alone
options.C: Outcome, budget, team, and a weekly report to the store manager
options.D: Task, deadline, warning, and who the owner must report to daily

questions.stem: Your team leader now owns the rota. Who does the course say answers for it?

options.A: You do: the outcome is theirs to run, and yours to answer for
options.B: The team leader does, since the rota is now fully their responsibility
options.C: The area manager does, since they approved the change in ownership
options.D: Nobody in particular, as long as the rota is published on time

questions.stem: You coach your assistant manager after watching a team briefing. How many behaviors does the course say to work on in one coaching loop?

options.A: Three, so the conversation covers everything you saw in the briefing
options.B: As many as you noticed, written down so nothing is missed
options.C: One, because a single clear behavior feels doable
options.D: None yet; wait until you have watched several more briefings

questions.stem: How does the course say a one-to-one with a leader should end?

options.A: With a general catch-up on how the leader is feeling about the week and the team
options.B: With you taking the leader's problems away to solve them yourself
options.C: With a list of every issue raised, sent by email afterwards
options.D: With a decision or a priority line, restated in the leader's own words

questions.stem: Which of these belongs in a record of a performance conversation?

options.A: Your view of why the team member keeps doing it, and what it says about them
options.B: The names of the colleagues who complained about the team member's work
options.C: The observed behavior, the date, what was agreed, and the next check date
options.D: A note about the team member's private life, in case it explains the gap

questions.stem: You open a second conversation about the same gap. Which opener fits the course?

options.A: "I need to warn you that this could become formal if it does not stop."
options.B: "You're late again. Honestly, I don't know what's going on with you."
options.C: "You have already had a warning about this, so you know how serious it is."
options.D: "It seems like this has been a difficult few weeks, and I want to be honest about what I've seen."

questions.stem: A team member breaks a safety rule. Applying the course's questions, what do you have, and what do you do?

options.A: A performance gap: coach them in a one-to-one and agree a check date
options.B: A conduct case: hand it to your manager or HR, with the facts and what you did
options.C: A performance gap: give a warning yourself so it does not happen again
options.D: A conduct case: keep it to yourself so the team member is not embarrassed in front of others

questions.stem: A team member has several recurring issues. How does the course say to handle them?

options.A: One behavior per conversation; the pattern shows in repeated dated entries
options.B: Raise all of them in one meeting, so the person sees the full picture
options.C: Raise them only at the yearly review, so the team member is not overwhelmed
options.D: Ask the team member to list their own issues before you raise any of them

questions.stem: What is the order of the three-step recovery for a significant complaint?

options.A: Name the feeling with a soft opener, fix the practical problem, then one named follow-up
options.B: Fix the practical problem, explain the policy, then name the customer's feeling
options.C: Apologize, offer compensation, then name the feeling with a soft opener
options.D: Name the feeling, explain why it happened, then ask if the customer is happy

questions.stem: A customer asks for compensation above the amount you can approve. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Approve it anyway, since keeping the customer happy matters most
options.B: Tell the customer there is nothing you can do and close the matter
options.C: Escalate, and tell the customer what happens next and by when
options.D: Offer a smaller amount in your limit and say that is the final offer

questions.stem: Which three questions does the one-page disruption plan answer?

options.A: What went wrong, whose fault it was, and how much it cost the store
options.B: Who takes charge, what the customer hears, and what is paused
options.C: When head office is told, which form is used, and who signs it
options.D: Which team members are on shift, who is on break, and who is off

questions.stem: A team member says a great recovery always turns an upset customer into a more loyal one. What does the course say?

options.A: That is right, so every complaint is a chance to win more loyalty than before
options.B: That is wrong, because a recovery never changes how the customer feels
options.C: That is right, as long as the customer also gets some compensation for the trouble they had
options.D: A good recovery rebuilds trust, but does not guarantee more loyalty than no problem

questions.stem: What four parts does the one-page management review contain?

options.A: Effort, achievements, team mood, and any thoughts from the area manager
options.B: Every number in the report, the rota, the complaints log, and a request
options.C: A summary of the week, a list of problems, a forecast for next month, and a thank-you to the team
options.D: The outcome, the numbers that matter, what blocks you, and the decision you need

questions.stem: Which closing line fits an update to your area manager?

options.A: "What do you need from me to decide on the temporary hours by the 20th?"
options.B: "Let me know if you have any thoughts on all of this when you get a chance."
options.C: "Any feedback on the week is welcome, whenever you have time to read it."
options.D: "I think that covers everything for now. Speak soon."

questions.stem: Your area manager visits next week. What does the course say earns trust?

options.A: A polished floor, chosen team members and a rehearsed walk-through
options.B: Evidence ready, pointing at what you see, and the same story when questioned
options.C: A short presentation on slides that covers all of the store's good results from the last quarter
options.D: Keeping problems off the walk-through so the visit stays positive

questions.stem: A head office display plan is causing queues at your entrance. How does the course say to disagree?

options.A: Explain that the plan clearly was not tested in a real store
options.B: Quietly move the display and tell head office afterwards
options.C: Name a shared goal, give your evidence, propose one change, and ask what they need
options.D: Ask head office to cancel the plan for every store in the area

questions.stem: Your routines keep fading when your attention moves elsewhere. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Check every routine yourself each day, so nothing is missed
options.B: Add more routines, so the important ones are covered several times by different people
options.C: Write each one as a priority line with an owner and a check date, three at most
options.D: Remind the team about all routines at every morning huddle

questions.stem: In your store record, why does the course say to name the behavior behind each number?

options.A: It makes the record longer, which shows the area manager more effort
options.B: A number with no behavior behind it looks like luck, not management
options.C: It lets you leave out the numbers that did not improve this year
options.D: It shows which team members to thank in the promotion case

questions.stem: You are choosing a successor. What does the course say to look for?

options.A: The strongest performer on the till, since results show who is ready
options.B: The longest-serving team member, since experience matters most
options.C: Whoever asks for the role first, since that shows motivation
options.D: Observable behaviors: calm under pressure, follow-up without chasing, explaining a standard

questions.stem: You present your promotion case to your area manager. Which closing line fits the course?

options.A: "What would you need to see over the next quarter to feel confident recommending this?"
options.B: "I think I deserve this. Will you put my name forward?"
options.C: "Can you promise me the next opening, given my results?"
options.D: "Do you agree that I am ready for the next step now?"

questions.stem: Several months into the role, which three things is an Area Manager judged on?

options.A: The hours worked each week, the speed of replies to messages, and the number of unit visits completed each month.
options.B: Area results with context, the development of unit managers, and customer consistency across units.
options.C: The targets the Area Manager hits personally, the size of the area, and the number of problems solved alone.
options.D: How well every problem that reached the Area Manager's desk was handled, and how satisfied senior leaders seem.

questions.stem: While writing a baseline, an Area Manager realizes there is no observed example at all for one unit manager. What should go in that manager's read?

options.A: A read based on the general impression the manager gave in the last area meeting everyone attended.
options.B: The same read as the strongest manager in the area, so that the baseline does not look incomplete.
options.C: A cautious negative read, so that any later problem in that unit will not come as a surprise.
options.D: "No evidence yet", followed by a visit to observe.

questions.stem: A regional director asks how the area is doing. Which reply meets the course's standard?

options.A: "One unit is at 92 against a target of 100 for two months. Full cover last month did not close the gap, so I am visiting Thursday to test two causes. Would a one-page summary after the visit, or the answer in our next call, help you most?"
options.B: "It's going well overall. One unit is slightly behind because of staffing trouble, and I'm working on it."
options.C: "All the units are fine. I'll let you know straight away if anything changes that you need to hear about."
options.D: "One unit is behind, and honestly that is down to its manager. Is it all right if I deal with it my way?"

questions.stem: Which tool is a written statement for one manager of what you will do and will not do to support them, agreed in a meeting?

options.A: A coaching plan, which records the support the Area Manager promises for the year ahead.
options.B: A support allocation plan, which lists how the Area Manager's time is shared between units.
options.C: A support boundary.
options.D: A decisions-needed list, which sets out what the unit manager must decide alone.

questions.stem: Which five elements make up the weekly area rhythm?

options.A: Unit visits, manager check-ins, time for the repeating gap, customer follow-up, and escalation.
options.B: Unit visits, team briefings, stock checks, a weekly report to senior leaders, and a monthly area meeting.
options.C: Planning, unit visits, cover for absent managers, complaint handling, and a review of every unit's figures.
options.D: Manager check-ins, recruitment, training sessions, customer calls, and a written summary for each unit.

questions.stem: During a unit visit, a customer walks up to you and asks about a delayed order while the unit manager is standing nearby. What should you do?

options.A: Take over the order yourself so that the customer sees a senior person handling it properly.
options.B: Tell the customer you are only visiting today and that someone from the unit will help shortly.
options.C: Ask the customer why they are unhappy, so that you can judge how the unit has handled it so far.
options.D: Answer in two short sentences, then stop and let the unit manager take the rest of the conversation.

questions.stem: How should every manager check-in close?

options.A: With a list of five improvements for the manager to work through before the next visit.
options.B: With a detailed summary of everything the Area Manager noticed during the whole visit.
options.C: With one agreed action, one owner and one date, written down.
options.D: With a request for a full written report from the manager by the end of the week.

questions.stem: The same booking error has now appeared in three units, and fixing it needs a decision you cannot make. What three things should your escalation carry?

options.A: The names of the staff involved, your opinion of each one, and a deadline for them to improve.
options.B: The evidence, your recommendation, and the date a decision is needed.
options.C: A promise already given to the units, a summary of complaints, and a request for extra headcount.
options.D: The history of the problem, an apology for raising it, and a question about whether to carry on.

questions.stem: Two reports show different numbers for the same measure in one unit. What is the right question to ask?

options.A: Which of the two reports is wrong, so that it can be corrected before the next review meeting.
options.B: Which number is better for the unit, so that it can be used in the area summary this period.
options.C: What each report counts: how it defines the period and what it excludes.
options.D: Which unit manager entered the figures, so that the person responsible can be asked to explain.

questions.stem: According to the course, a target gap asks four questions. Which four?

options.A: Size, trend, context and cause.
options.B: Size, blame, deadline and the consequence for the unit manager.
options.C: Target, effort, attitude and the manager's length of service.
options.D: Cost, speed, ranking against other units and a recovery date.

questions.stem: You want to compare two units fairly on one measure. What do you do?

options.A: Take the unit with the higher number as the standard and ask the other manager to explain the whole difference.
options.B: Check both define the measure the same way, adjust for the obvious differences, then look at what remains.
options.C: Compare every available measure at once, so that no difference between the two units can be missed.
options.D: Ask each manager to describe their own number without any data, then decide which account sounds stronger.

questions.stem: One unit is far ahead of the others on a measure. What is the most useful response?

options.A: Leave the unit alone, since a unit that is ahead of target has no problem that needs solving.
options.B: Raise that unit's target straight away so that the gap to the other units looks smaller.
options.C: Tell every other unit to copy the practice from next week, before the advantage is lost.
options.D: Ask how the manager runs the week, check whether the practice holds, and consider a limited pilot in one other willing unit.

questions.stem: Which of these matters sits with the Area Manager to handle, rather than with the employer's people process?

options.A: A concern about a unit manager's conduct towards a member of the team.
options.B: A situation that involves a unit manager's health or personal circumstances.
options.C: Any matter that could carry a formal consequence for the unit manager.
options.D: A unit manager's skill gap in building the weekend rota.

questions.stem: What are the three parts of a support boundary?

options.A: What the manager did wrong, what will happen if it repeats, and when it will be reviewed.
options.B: What you will do, what you will not do, and what the manager will do.
options.C: What the target is, what the gap is, and what reward follows if the gap is closed in time.
options.D: What senior leaders expect, what HR requires, and what the manager must sign to confirm it.

questions.stem: A unit manager has a clear standard, a named barrier and a written checkpoint, and has missed the checkpoint again with nothing changed. What next?

options.A: Have the same conversation once more, but this time more firmly and with a shorter deadline attached.
options.B: Quietly take the work back yourself for a few weeks so that the unit's numbers are protected.
options.C: Stop repeating the conversation and move to process: the support boundary, a factual dated record, then escalation with a recommendation.
options.D: Tell the manager that a formal warning will follow if the checkpoint is missed one more time.

questions.stem: Before escalating a manager who agrees every time and then does not change, which two things should you check?

options.A: Whether the standard was stated in a form they could act on, and whether the barrier is skill, will or circumstance.
options.B: Whether the manager likes working for you, and whether the rest of the unit team supports the manager.
options.C: Whether other Area Managers have the same problem with their managers, and whether the target could be lowered for this one unit.
options.D: Whether the manager has been warned in writing before, and whether a replacement manager is available now.

questions.stem: When you ask a shared function for help, the ask stands on evidence. What three things does that evidence mean?

options.A: The specific problem, what it costs, and what you have already tried inside your own authority.
options.B: How urgent the problem feels, who above you wants it fixed, and how long you have already been waiting.
options.C: The names of the people at fault, the complaints received, and the deadline you have set for the fix.
options.D: Your area's results, your own workload this month, and the support other areas have already received.

questions.stem: Which team should a limited pilot be run with?

options.A: The worst-performing unit, because it has the most to gain from a new practice.
options.B: Every unit in the area at once, so that the result is large enough to be trusted.
options.C: One willing team, not the worst-performing unit.
options.D: The unit with the newest manager, because new managers accept change most easily.

questions.stem: In a support allocation plan, who is named on the 'owner' line?

options.A: The Area Manager, because the Area Manager raised the problem.
options.B: The unit manager whose unit has the most cases of the problem.
options.C: The senior leader who will be told if the support does not arrive.
options.D: The person in the other function who agreed to the commitment.

questions.stem: A four-week pilot with a shared function ends and the agreed success measure has not moved. What should you do?

options.A: Present the result in the best possible light, so that the other function stays willing to help next time.
options.B: Say so plainly to the other function, bring back the next diagnostic question, and decide together whether to stop, adjust or try a different response.
options.C: Let the pilot end quietly without a report, since there is no improvement worth sharing with anyone.
options.D: Extend the pilot to all units anyway, because four weeks is too short to judge any new practice.

questions.stem: What is an area review for?

options.A: Presenting every measure for every unit, so that senior leaders are fully informed.
options.B: Making the decisions only senior leaders can make.
options.C: Showing senior leaders that the area is improving and that no help is needed.
options.D: Giving each unit manager a chance to explain their own results to senior leaders.

questions.stem: What belongs on a decisions-needed list?

options.A: Two or three decisions above your authority, each with your recommendation and the date needed.
options.B: Every open issue in the area, listed in order of urgency, so that senior leaders can choose which ones to take on.
options.C: Your own operating choices for the next period, so that senior leaders can approve each of them in advance.
options.D: The decisions the unit managers want made, passed on exactly as they were raised and without a view of your own.

questions.stem: In a review, a senior leader says, "I'm not convinced that store needs temporary staff." What should you do?

options.A: Defend the figure point by point until the leader accepts that the recommendation was right.
options.B: Withdraw the request at once and say that the area will manage without the extra cover.
options.C: Ask whether the leader is willing to approve it anyway, so that the meeting can move on.
options.D: Name the concern plainly with no "but", say what not deciding would cost, then ask what they would need to see to approve it by the date.

questions.stem: Which four parts make up the one-page area review summary?

options.A: Results for every unit, a ranking of the unit managers, complaints by customer name, and next year's targets.
options.B: A summary of visits made, hours worked in each unit, problems solved, and requests from the unit managers.
options.C: Results against target with context, customer-facing risks, decisions needed, and what happens next.
options.D: Good news first, the area's achievements, thanks to the teams, and a general note on the challenges ahead.

questions.stem: An escalated customer asks you for a refund above the level you can approve. Which reply follows the course?

options.A: "Don't worry, I'll make sure this is sorted out for you as soon as I possibly can."
options.B: "I'll approve it now and clear it with head office afterwards. Is that all right?"
options.C: "That is not possible under our policy, so there is nothing more I can do here."
options.D: "I cannot approve that from where I sit. I will bring your request, with my recommendation, to the person who can decide, by the fourteenth."

questions.stem: Which opening line should you use with a customer whose problem has been escalated to you?

options.A: "I can see you're frustrated, and I completely understand how you feel."
options.B: "I understand you're upset, but the branch did follow the correct process."
options.C: "This has taken longer than it should have."
options.D: "Why did you not raise this with the branch manager before coming to me?"

questions.stem: After an escalation, which debrief with the unit manager follows the course?

options.A: "You need to be much more careful with customers. This one should never have reached me."
options.B: "On the twelfth, the call about the delayed order ended without a date for an update. The customer called me two days later. Let's practice closing that call with a dated next step."
options.C: "I think you didn't call back because you find this customer difficult. Am I right?"
options.D: "The customer was unreasonable, so let's not worry. These things happen in every unit."

questions.stem: When is the recovery of an escalated case finished?

options.A: When the fix has happened and the customer has confirmed it in their own words.
options.B: When the customer has calmed down and has agreed to wait for the next update from the unit.
options.C: When the promised date has been met, even if nobody has spoken to the customer since then.
options.D: When the unit manager reports that the case has been closed on the unit's own system.

questions.stem: A unit manager who was your peer until this year now reports to you, and things feel awkward. What does the course recommend?

options.A: Soften your feedback for the first few months so that the old friendship is protected.
options.B: Become more formal and firm from day one, to show that the promotion has changed things.
options.C: Sit down early, say plainly what the structure is now, name the awkwardness as a fact with no "but" after it, then pause.
options.D: Avoid the subject and let time settle it, since raising it would only make it worse.

questions.stem: Which part of SBI does the course say people most often skip?

options.A: The situation.
options.B: The behavior.
options.C: The practice task agreed with the person afterwards.
options.D: The impact.

questions.stem: In a coaching plan, who owns the practice task and who owns the checkpoint?

options.A: The manager owns the task; you own the checkpoint.
options.B: You own the task; the manager owns the checkpoint and reports on it.
options.C: You own both, so that nothing is missed while the manager is still learning.
options.D: The manager owns both, and you step back until the manager asks for help.

questions.stem: In which of these situations should you step in rather than coach?

options.A: A manager's handover notes keep missing the late-delivery list.
options.B: A safety risk in the unit.
options.C: A manager asks customers the same thin discovery question each time.
options.D: A manager gives vague feedback to their own team after a busy shift.

questions.stem: How should the units on an area priority and risk map be ranked?

options.A: By how likely the risk is to harm a customer, and how soon.
options.B: By how loudly each unit manager raises concerns with the Area Manager.
options.C: By the size of each unit's revenue, with the largest unit always first.
options.D: By how long it has been since the Area Manager last visited each unit.

questions.stem: Which line belongs in an Area Manager's written record?

options.A: "The manager seemed overwhelmed and is probably not coping with the pressure of the role."
options.B: "A customer, named with her phone number, complained at the service desk about a refund."
options.C: "I told the manager that a formal warning will follow if the queue is not fixed."
options.D: "On Tuesday the queue reached the door for the second morning running."

questions.stem: On a visit you find a unit has quietly invented its own way of completing a task. How does the course say to treat it?

options.A: As defiance of the standard, to be corrected with the unit manager on the same day.
options.B: As a symptom that the official way may have stopped working: name it as a symptom and ask what it is telling you.
options.C: As a sign of initiative, to be praised and copied to the other units straight away.
options.D: As a small local habit that does not need to be noted or followed up at all.

questions.stem: You spot a risk on a unit visit. When does the course say it counts as managed?

options.A: When the unit manager has said that it is nothing to worry about this month.
options.B: When you have mentioned it to the unit manager before leaving the building.
options.C: When it is fixed, escalated or watched with a clear date.
options.D: When it has not appeared again on your next visit to the same unit.

questions.stem: Which four parts make up the record behind a promotion case?

options.A: Length of service, hours worked, the size of the area, and praise received from unit managers.
options.B: Targets hit, costs cut, complaints avoided, and the number of visits made to each unit during the whole of the year.
options.C: Results with context, managers you developed, escalations you handled, and risks you kept small.
options.D: Results alone, a list of managers' names, awards received, and a statement of your ambitions.

questions.stem: Why does the course say to update the record every month rather than assemble it the week before a promotion conversation?

options.A: A monthly record is longer, and a longer record always carries more weight with senior leaders.
options.B: A monthly record reads as a pattern; one assembled in a week reads as a campaign.
options.C: Senior leaders check the dates on every entry and reject any record that was written late.
options.D: A record written every month no longer needs to include context for the results it shows.

questions.stem: How should the record describe a unit manager who improved with your coaching?

options.A: Describe what the manager achieved and what you did to support it, without claiming the achievement.
options.B: Present the improvement as your own result, since it would not have happened without your coaching at all.
options.C: Leave the manager out entirely, so that the record stays focused on your own results and decisions.
options.D: Include the manager's private circumstances, so that senior leaders understand how hard the change was.

questions.stem: Which item does the course call the important one in a handover?

options.A: A statement that everything in the area has been fully documented.
options.B: A full history of every problem the area has had since you started.
options.C: A list of the reasons why you are ready for the next-level role.
options.D: The one or two things that only you currently know.

questions.stem: A manager three months into the role wants to judge honestly whether they are performing strongly. Which basis does the course say to use?

options.A: The number of hours they put in each week and how busy the team looks to people outside it.
options.B: Whether the team likes them and whether their own manager seems pleased with them in meetings.
options.C: Evidence: numbers they can explain, usable feedback, decisions inside their authority, honest reporting, cross-team work and a factual record.
options.D: How long and detailed their weekly reports are, since more detail shows the manager is in control.

questions.stem: A newly promoted manager tells a colleague: "Now that I have the title, the team will trust my calls." Which response reflects the course?

options.A: Credibility comes from what you do, observed over time, not from the title.
options.B: The title gives full credibility for the first few months, and after that results take over as the main measure of trust.
options.C: Credibility comes mainly from product knowledge, so the manager should show technical expertise in every meeting they run.
options.D: Credibility is decided in the annual review, so day-to-day behavior matters much less than the formal rating it produces.

questions.stem: Which four parts make up the four-part decision for communicating a decision downward?

options.A: The decision, the people affected by it, the risks involved, and the deadline for raising objections.
options.B: The problem, the options considered, the team's vote on them, and the final ruling from senior management.
options.C: The decision, the person who approved it, the budget it needs, and how its results will be reported upward.
options.D: The decision, the why, what is fixed versus flexible, and what is next.

questions.stem: A manager runs the Gray Area Test on a borderline way of recording a deal and is still unsure whether it is acceptable. What does the course say to do?

options.A: Go ahead if no customer is directly harmed, and note the decision in the record afterwards.
options.B: Ask before acting, because that is what escalation is for.
options.C: Follow what other managers in the business usually do, since common practice shows what is acceptable.
options.D: Delay the decision until the end of the period, when the figures will show whether it really mattered.

questions.stem: A manager's weekly one-to-ones keep turning into a round of status updates on every account. What does the course recommend?

options.A: Make the meeting longer so the updates and the coaching both fit into the time available.
options.B: Ask for the update in writing beforehand and spend the meeting on the one thing that will change the number.
options.C: Cancel the one-to-one in busy weeks and rely on the written report to cover the updates.
options.D: Collect all the updates first, then add feedback at the end of the meeting if time allows.

questions.stem: In SBI, which of these lines describes observable behavior?

options.A: "You were careless on that call, and it showed in how the client reacted afterwards."
options.B: "You don't seem as committed to following up with your clients as you were before."
options.C: "You need to be much more proactive with clients from now on, on every single call."
options.D: "The call ended without a date for the next conversation."

questions.stem: Which commitment meets the course's test for a measurable commitment?

options.A: "Every call logged with a next step by end of day; the manager spot-checks five on Friday."
options.B: "Work harder on follow-up this week and keep the manager informed about how it is going."
options.C: "Focus more on quality conversations and try to improve the overall health of the pipeline."
options.D: "Make follow-up a top priority this month and give it far more attention than last month."

questions.stem: A team member's calls are made but never logged, and the same gap has repeated for four weeks. What is the best move this week?

options.A: Repeat the instruction to log every call more firmly and set a stricter daily deadline for doing it.
options.B: Add a second and a third commitment to the same meeting so the person has more chances to show change.
options.C: Name the pattern, then ask what makes logging hard and what would have to change on your side.
options.D: Issue a formal warning straight away so the person fully understands how serious the gap has become.

questions.stem: A manager feels a target set for the team is unreachable. What is the most useful first question to ask?

options.A: Whether the team likes the target enough to commit to it fully for the rest of the period.
options.B: How the figures could be presented so that the target looks closer than it currently is.
options.C: Whether it is better to wait until the end of the quarter before raising any concern about it.
options.D: Which assumption the target rests on, and whether that assumption still holds.

questions.stem: In what order should a weekly report to your manager answer its three questions?

options.A: What the result was, what moved it, and what you will do.
options.B: What the team did, how hard it worked, and what result came out of that effort.
options.C: What you will do next, what moved the result, and finally what the result actually was.
options.D: What went wrong, who was responsible for it, and what the result was at the end of the week.

questions.stem: This week the number of proposals your team sent rose sharply, while completed deals fell. Which reading matches the course?

options.A: Activity is up, so the team is clearly working harder, and the results will follow in the next few weeks.
options.B: The fall in deals is just noise, so the rise in proposals should be the headline of the weekly report.
options.C: Effort rose while outcomes fell, which points to quality or fit; ask what changed in how proposals are chosen.
options.D: Proposals are an outcome signal, so the week should be reported as a strong result for the team overall.

questions.stem: Your team's monthly total looks strong, but most of it came from one person. Which misleading pattern is the manager at risk of missing?

options.A: A rate without its base, which is only a problem when the number of opportunities is very large.
options.B: A pooled total can hide that most people performed below the middle.
options.C: A shifted measure, because a strong total almost always means the definition of a deal was changed.
options.D: A short spike, because one strong person always means the team's underlying trend is falling.

questions.stem: A team member says a large deal will close this month because the customer "loved the proposal." What should the manager ask?

options.A: "What did the customer do last week that they hadn't done the week before?"
options.B: "Why do you think the customer loved the proposal so much this time around?"
options.C: "Are you completely sure it will close this month, or should we be more careful with it?"
options.D: "When exactly will you close it, so that I can put the full amount into my number?"

questions.stem: Before a forecast leaves your desk, how should each assumption behind a significant deal be marked?

options.A: Likely, possible or unlikely, based on how the last meeting with the customer felt.
options.B: Hot, warm or cold, depending on how confident the team member sounds about the deal.
options.C: Checked, unchecked or doubtful.
options.D: Early, middle or late stage, according to how long the deal has sat in the pipeline.

questions.stem: How should each line of the risk list you prepare before a forecast review be structured?

options.A: Risk, owner, a probability score and the expected loss to the total if it happens.
options.B: Risk, background, who caused it and how it could be avoided the next time it comes up.
options.C: Risk, the team member's opinion of it, the customer's mood and a fallback deal to use.
options.D: Risk, evidence, action, date.

questions.stem: A large deal slips from this month to next. Your manager asks what happened. Which reply follows the course?

options.A: Give a revised total straight away, even an estimate, so your manager is not left without any figure.
options.B: Say what changed, its effect on the number, what you are doing and when you will confirm.
options.C: Wait until the new number is fully certain before saying anything, so you only ever report confirmed facts.
options.D: Promise that another deal will come in to cover the gap, so the month's total still holds as forecast.

questions.stem: A team member has missed the weekly call target for four weeks. Which opening best fits a first underperformance conversation?

options.A: "Your attitude has slipped lately, and I need you to commit to doing better from next week."
options.B: "Why have your numbers dropped? I need a clear answer from you before we go any further."
options.C: "I want to talk about the account calls. The log shows about half the weekly target for four weeks, and some follow-ups have slipped. What has been in the way?"
options.D: "I'm putting this in writing as a first warning so that you know how serious this is."

questions.stem: Which of these should a sales manager escalate to HR rather than handle alone as a performance conversation?

options.A: A team member reports that a colleague may be bullying them.
options.B: A team member has missed the weekly call target for three weeks in a row and has not yet been spoken to.
options.C: A team member's follow-ups are slipping because the handoff to another department keeps breaking down.
options.D: A former peer keeps treating the weekly one-to-one as a casual chat between equals instead of a meeting.

questions.stem: A team member's missed calls seem to come from a broken handoff between two systems. What should the manager do first?

options.A: Keep correcting the person's activity level with SBI each week until the handoff is eventually fixed by someone.
options.B: Check whether the process is really the cause, own the fix if it is, then name the behavior needed.
options.C: Escalate the matter to HR immediately so that the policy side of the problem is covered from the very start.
options.D: Tell the person to find their own way around the handoff so that the targets are still hit this month.

questions.stem: After a first underperformance conversation, what should the manager's written record contain?

options.A: A short summary of the person's attitude and character, so that any later manager has the full context.
options.B: Any personal details the person shared in the meeting, so that the complete picture is kept on file.
options.C: A clear promise about hours, pay or warnings, so that the person knows exactly where they stand now.
options.D: Date, what was discussed, what was agreed and what is next, factual and work-related only.

questions.stem: A customer escalates to you, speaking fast and loudly. What should you do first?

options.A: Ask the customer to calm down first, so that the rest of the conversation can stay productive and focused.
options.B: Ask the customer why they are so upset, so that the real reason behind the complaint comes out quickly.
options.C: Transfer the call straight to your own manager, so that a more senior person is involved from the start.
options.D: Listen to the end without interrupting, then play the situation back in their words.

questions.stem: You have taken a customer escalation yourself. When should your own manager first hear about it?

options.A: Once the case is fully resolved, so that you can report a finished outcome to them rather than an open problem.
options.B: From you, before the customer can raise it with them, so they never decide anything about the case blind.
options.C: Only if the customer asks to speak to someone more senior than you at some point during the case.
options.D: At the next weekly review, where all of the team's open cases are discussed together in one place.

questions.stem: What three parts must a next step agreed with an escalated customer contain?

options.A: What will happen, who will do it, and by when.
options.B: An apology, a goodwill gesture and a firm promise that the same problem will not happen again.
options.C: The cause of the problem, the person at fault for it and the company policy that applies to the case.
options.D: A summary of the complaint, the manager's own view of it and a final decision given on the same call.

questions.stem: A customer asks for a credit that sits above your authority. Which reply follows the course?

options.A: "I'm sure we can sort something out for you on the credit, so just leave it with me."
options.B: "Let me offer you a smaller credit that I can approve for you right now instead."
options.C: "I can't approve that myself. I'll take it to my manager today and come back to you by Thursday with the answer, whatever it is."
options.D: "My manager will never approve that amount, so there's really no point in asking."

questions.stem: A written agreement with another team is most likely to hold when it covers which four parts?

options.A: The goal of the project, the meeting schedule, the budget, and the escalation route if the plan fails.
options.B: What the other team provides, by when, in what form, and who owns it on each side.
options.C: Each team's priorities, the risks involved, the manager who approved it, and a date to review it.
options.D: The request, the reason behind it, the deadline, and the consequence for the other team if it is missed.

questions.stem: An input from another team has not arrived and your week depends on it. Which question is most likely to surface the real constraint?

options.A: "What would have to happen on your side for this to move this week?"
options.B: "What is the current status of the input, and roughly when do you think we can expect to receive it?"
options.C: "Why is this late again, when we all agreed on the date together at the last cross-team meeting?"
options.D: "Could you please make sure it gets to me by Wednesday at the latest, so my team is not held up?"

questions.stem: The quality team says your team's process is sloppy; your team says quality checks slow everything down. What does the course say your job is?

options.A: Decide which team is right and back that team firmly in front of both groups so the conflict ends.
options.B: Escalate the conflict to your manager at once so that it is settled from above before it grows.
options.C: Tell your own team that the quality team is the problem, so that your people feel fully supported.
options.D: Find what each side is protecting and make a shared measure visible.

questions.stem: Two of your senior people return from a cross-team meeting saying the other function is deliberately blocking them. What do you say first?

options.A: "You're right, they've never been helpful to us. Let's plan our work around them from now on."
options.B: "I'll escalate this to my manager right away so that they know exactly what has been going on."
options.C: "Tell me exactly what was said and what outcome each side needs."
options.D: "Let's stop inviting them to our meetings until they show they are willing to cooperate with us."

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a status readout and a working session?

options.A: A working session tests evidence and ends in owned decisions; a readout only moves information upward.
options.B: A working session lasts longer and covers more accounts in more detail than a readout ever does.
options.C: A readout includes the whole team, while a working session is always held one to one with each person.
options.D: A working session has no fixed agenda, so people can raise anything they want during the meeting.

questions.stem: In what order should the five parts of a review meeting run?

options.A: The loop from last time, numbers, what we stop, quality cases, decisions and owners.
