options.B: Quality cases, numbers, what we stop, decisions and owners, the loop from last time.
options.C: Numbers in one screen, quality cases, decisions and owners, the loop from last time, what we stop.
options.D: Numbers, the loop from last time, decisions and owners, quality cases, what we stop.

questions.stem: Your review meeting is running over time. Which part should you cut first?

options.A: The quality cases, because they take the longest and can safely move to next week's review.
options.B: The numbers, because they can be read; judgment needs the room.
options.C: The loop from last time, because last week's decisions are already written down for everyone.
options.D: What we stop, because it is the least important part of the meeting and can be done by email.

questions.stem: A decision from last week's review was not carried out. How should the manager open the item?

options.A: Ask the room who was responsible for the missed item first, so that ownership is clear from the start.
options.B: Skip the item if time is short and pick it up at the person's next one-to-one meeting instead.
options.C: Ask the owner to explain why it was missed and write their reason into the meeting notes.
options.D: Read the decision back, then ask what got in the way before asking who is responsible.

questions.stem: According to the course, what does keeping your job as a manager mainly rest on?

options.A: Producing a few brilliant weeks with standout results that senior people will remember for a long time.
options.B: Working visibly longer hours than your team so that everyone can see how committed you are to the job.
options.C: Reliable delivery of what your employer measures, and telling your manager early when something will not happen.
options.D: Keeping every problem quiet until it is solved, so that you always look capable to the people above you.

questions.stem: Why does the course say people often delay escalating a problem?

options.A: They feel reluctant to pass on bad news.
options.B: Their employer's policy usually forbids escalation until a problem has been fully solved by the team.
options.C: Most problems sort themselves out if they are left alone for a week or two, so waiting is normal.
options.D: Escalating too often is the main reason that new managers lose their jobs in the first year.

questions.stem: A neighboring team asks to borrow your best performer for two days during your peak week. Which reply follows the course?

options.A: "Of course, take them for both days. Good relations with your team matter more than our numbers this week."
options.B: "No, we can't spare anyone this week, and I'd rather you didn't approach my team directly again."
options.C: "It's up to them. Ask them yourself and let them decide whether they can fit it in this week."
options.D: "I want to help, and this week would cost us two renewals we've committed to. Which suits your timeline better, the following Monday or the Wednesday after?"

questions.stem: Why does a late, resentful no damage trust more than an early, calm one?

options.A: People always welcome an early no, whatever the reason or the timing behind it happens to be.
options.B: Agreement followed by resentment takes back trust already spent.
options.C: Targets change every week, so a late answer is usually out of date by the time it is given.
options.D: A no only counts when it is given in writing and copied to the manager of the person asking.

questions.stem: According to the course, promotion most reliably depends on which three things?

options.A: Long tenure in the role, a heavy visible workload and strong support from colleagues on other teams.
options.B: Evidence of results, evidence of judgment and a widening scope of trust.
options.C: Being the busiest person on the team, saying yes to every task and showing loyalty to your manager.
options.D: Starting to do the next job early, high visibility with senior people and a good annual rating.

questions.stem: Which entry belongs in a manager's promotion record?

options.A: "Ran great review meetings all quarter that the whole team really seemed to enjoy attending."
options.B: "Showed consistently strong leadership, an excellent attitude and real commitment to the team."
options.C: "Covered a hard customer case for a colleague and noted the details of their personal situation."
options.D: "Ran the weekly review every week from the start of the quarter; follow-ups now close on the day agreed."

questions.stem: You are ready to ask about the next level. Which question should open the promotion conversation?

options.A: "What would need to be true for me to be considered for the next-level role at the next review?"
options.B: "I think I'm ready for the next step now. What do you think?"
options.C: "Would you put me forward for the next-level role? I'd love your support."
options.D: "I've been doing really well lately. Can you promise me the role this year?"

questions.stem: Your manager says, "It's not the right time. Let's talk again in a few months." What is the strongest next move?

options.A: Accept the answer and pause the record until the next conversation has been booked in the diary.
options.B: Ask for a firm promise of promotion next quarter, so that there is a clear date to work towards.
options.C: Ask what would need to be true, by when, and how you will both know it has happened.
options.D: Ask a senior colleague to raise your case with your manager on your behalf before the next review.
